atoms.t: Lesson 1
Prepare for tonight
A journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step.
Lao Tzu
Part 1
The smaller decision
It’s late. Your phone is beside you, and you’re making another promise about never watching porn again. You might mean every word.
But at midnight, the useful decision is smaller: what will you do with the phone before you go to sleep?
Put it somewhere you can’t reach from bed. Check the alarm first. If you need to receive urgent calls, keep those available.
A shelf across the room is enough if leaving it outside the bedroom would cause problems. Put the laptop away too. Otherwise, you’ve moved one screen and left another waiting.

steps: Get into bed to answer a message

atoms.t: Part 2
An earlier moment
Think of the evening that usually goes wrong. You get into bed to answer a message. Then you check a feed. Twenty minutes later, you’re searching for something you had decided to stop watching.
By then, putting the phone down feels much harder. Charging it elsewhere changes an earlier decision, before that search begins.
This won’t make every urge disappear. It gives you a few seconds in which you have to get up and choose.

Use those seconds to begin something you’ve already decided on: wash, read a few pages, or turn out the light. Another search for recovery advice can wait until tomorrow if it keeps you awake beside the same screen.
Marcus Aurelius reminded himself to deal with the trouble in front of him instead of carrying every possible future trouble into it.
You can apply that idea tonight. You don’t have to settle the coming year before putting the phone down.
Part 3
Where you’re starting
Before you finish, write a few facts about where you’re starting. When do you usually watch? How much time does it take, if you know? What does it interrupt? What tends to happen afterwards?
Approximate answers are useful. Guessing precise numbers isn’t. You’ll return to these notes later to see what changed. Tonight, they only need to be honest.
Well begun is half done.
Aristotle
Today’s task
Prepare for tonight
Start one private note called My recovery plan.

Write your porn boundary and what you know about your starting point: when you usually watch, roughly how often or for how long, what it interrupts, and what you do after an urge or slip. Write “unknown” where needed.
Prepare tonight: set the alarm, put the phone out of reach from bed, and put other devices away.
Keep needed calls and accessibility available. If the device must stay close, close the content and choose a practical limit on browsing.
Your starting notes are saved and tonight’s device setup is ready.
Lesson complete.
One thing left today — the task.
Lesson 2
Remove easy access to porn
Begin at once to live, and count each separate day as a separate life.
Seneca
Part 1
Small conveniences
A bookmark saves you a few clicks. So does a familiar account, an open tab, or a folder you know by heart.
Those small conveniences matter when you’re tired and don’t want to think. Today, remove one that repeatedly brings you back to porn.

head: What you use
What to change
rows: Delete it without a last look

atoms.t: Start with what you actually use. If it’s a particular account, unfollow or block it. If it’s saved material, delete it without opening each item for a last look.
If the material is already gone, look at what still happens before you watch. Perhaps you keep opening the same feed in bed. Moving the charger may matter more than another hour of deleting files.
Part 2
What surrounds a habit
Wendy Wood and her colleagues studied students who moved to another university. Some habits changed when the surroundings changed; others carried over when familiar cues remained.
The study looked at everyday activities, not porn, and students weren’t randomly assigned to move. It suggests a useful place to look: the things around a habit that make it easy to repeat.
For example, clearing your desk won’t help much if the laptop still opens to the same account. Turning off its notifications might.
A blocker can add another obstacle, but check its settings without searching for sexual material. Keep access to work, calls, and anything else you need.
Part 3
Give it an ending
Give this job an ending. Twenty minutes is enough for a first pass.
You can spend a whole evening comparing blockers, organising folders, and calling it preparation. Stop when one change is in place. Then use the rest of the evening.
The change should be easy to describe: “I removed that account from my feed,” or “The charger is on the kitchen shelf.” Feeling determined is welcome, but it isn’t the thing you’ll check tomorrow.
Check whether the account stayed out of the feed or the phone stayed out of bed. If the change didn’t help, those details will tell you what to try next.
Question
What still makes porn easy to reach?
Choose all that fit. Choose F alone if it fits.

Remove easy access to porn

If there’s nothing relevant to remove, check yesterday’s device setup and fix any inconvenience. Write the useful change under Access in your plan.
You’ve made one useful change, or confirmed that the existing setup works. Stop there rather than browse for more things to delete.

Lesson 3
Choose where to go instead
An early-morning walk is a blessing for the whole day.
Henry David Thoreau
Part 1
Too many decisions
You decide to take a walk when you feel the urge. First, you check the weather. Then you choose a podcast, answer a message, and look for your shoes.
Ten minutes later, you’re still sitting with the phone. The walk was a reasonable idea. Starting it involved too many decisions.
Choose a nearby place now. That might be the corner shop, a short walk around the block, or the kitchen where someone else is sitting.
Know what you’ll do when you get there. “Go somewhere else” leaves another choice to make when you’re already struggling.
Part 2
Close it, then move
Close the content before you move. Taking the same search into a different room changes very little. Put the phone away, unless you need it for safety or access, and begin the activity you chose.
Make tea, sit with a book, or take the short walk. It can feel dull at first. The point is to stop spending the next ten minutes in the same search.
Check whether this works at the hour you need it. A café that’s open in the afternoon won’t help after midnight. A long walk may be impractical if you’re caring for a child.
In those cases, choose a room nearby. If moving is difficult, put the device farther away and bring a different activity within reach.
Part 3
Try it today
Try the steps today while you aren’t struggling with an urge. Find your shoes, check the door, and spend a few minutes in the place you chose.
Fix anything that makes starting awkward. This shows you can follow the steps; you’ll learn whether they help with an urge when one happens.
Decide what you’ll do when you return as well. Coming back to an open laptop can restart the search. Leave it closed and have the next activity ready, whether that’s food, work, or bed.
The walk doesn’t have to solve the whole evening. It should help you start the part that comes after it.
All truly great thoughts are conceived while walking.
Friedrich Nietzsche
Today’s task
Choose where to go instead
Name an exact place you can go when browsing starts: the kitchen table, a shared room, or a safe walk around the block. Try it for ten to twenty minutes today, after closing any triggering content.

If movement is limited, change your seat or put the device away and bring another activity within reach. Keep a phone when needed for safety or access. Save the place and first step under First response.
You’ve tried the change and saved the steps. If you can’t try it today, prepare an accessible option and choose when to try it.

Lesson 4
Prepare for sleep
There is a time for many words, and there is also a time for sleep.
Homer
Part 1
An evening with no ending
You finish a long day and want some time that’s yours. One video feels like a fair reward. Then another begins.
Eventually, the evening you wanted has taken the sleep you needed. Tomorrow starts with less energy, and the same bargain becomes tempting again.
Give entertainment an ending before you’re exhausted. A programme has a final episode; a feed usually doesn’t.

Choose when you’ll stop opening new things, where the phone will stay, and what you’ll do afterwards. If work ends late, build around that. Copying someone else’s early bedtime won’t make your shift shorter.
Part 2
Tiredness you stop noticing

In a controlled experiment, Hans Van Dongen and colleagues gave healthy adults restricted sleep opportunities over two weeks. Attention worsened across days in the groups allowed four or six hours in bed each night.
Their ratings of sleepiness didn’t fully track the decline. This was a sleep study, not a study of porn. It does show why “I’m used to being tired” deserves a second look.
An early alarm isn’t a repair for a very late night. Choose a wake time that leaves enough time for sleep.
If work or caring duties keep making that impossible, the problem may need practical help beyond a bedtime rule.
Part 3
After the phone goes away
Plan for being awake after the phone goes away. Leave a book nearby or choose something quiet you can listen to without opening a feed.
You can make sleep easier to start, but you can’t force yourself to fall asleep at a particular minute. Lying awake doesn’t cancel the work you did to end the browsing.
For the next few nights, notice what you can check: when browsing ended, where the phone stayed, and whether your schedule allowed time for sleep. On Day 7, you’ll look back at those details.
If the stopping time was unrealistic, change it. If sleep remains persistently difficult, seek qualified help rather than adding stricter alarms. Tonight’s job is to give sleep a fair chance.
Sleep that knits up the ravelled sleave of care.
William Shakespeare
Today’s task
Prepare for sleep
Plan the next sleep period. Choose a realistic wake time, when browsing ends, where the device goes, and a quiet activity before bed. Allow enough sleep for your circumstances.
If you can’t sleep, avoid restarting the feed in bed. Save the steps under Night routine and set a Day 7 reminder to check what happened.
The sleep plan and device setup are ready. Falling asleep on command isn’t part of the task.
Lesson complete.

Lesson 5
Have another activity ready
No great thing is created suddenly.
Epictetus
Part 1
What fits the hour
Stopping porn leaves a gap in the day. “Find a hobby” sounds sensible until it’s eleven at night and you have no idea what to begin. Choose something you can start at the hour you usually watch.
Ask what you need then. After a late shift, you might need food and rest. On an empty afternoon, you might want company or something interesting to do.
An activity can be enjoyable without improving you. A game with a friend, a meal, a walk, or a film can belong in your evening.
Part 2
Make it easier to begin
Katherine Milkman and her colleagues tested whether audiobooks could make gym visits more appealing. Participants in one group could listen to the supplied books only at the gym.
That group initially attended more often, but the advantage weakened over time, especially after a holiday break.
The experiment concerned exercise attendance, not recovery. Its useful idea is modest: making an activity enjoyable can make it easier to begin.
You can use that idea without making every pleasure a reward. Play music you like while cooking.
Pick a game you’d enjoy even if it did nothing for recovery. Food, sleep, and contact with people remain needs; don’t withhold them to prove commitment.
Prepare the first step. Put the ingredients out, leave the book on the chair, or agree on a time to play. The familiar habit already has an easy beginning. Your replacement needs one too.
Part 3
Try it and see
Try it for fifteen or twenty minutes today. Afterwards, ask what happened. Did you start? Did you enjoy it? Did it suit that particular hour?
Those are different questions. Cooking might work on Sunday and feel impossible after a late shift. Keep it for Sunday and choose something simpler for work nights.
If an activity helps once, try it again. If it doesn’t, change it. The gym study’s fading effect is a reminder to look beyond the first burst of interest.
You’re choosing things you’d like to keep doing after the novelty wears off.
No man is free who is not master of himself.
Epictetus
Today’s task
Have another activity ready
Choose an activity for the hour when you usually want porn. Match it to what you need: rest, interest, company, movement, or a break.

Prepare the materials and try it for fifteen to twenty minutes. Write whether it was easy to start and whether it helped you stop the usual browsing. Save it under Alternatives, with one adjustment if needed.
You’ve tried the activity and recorded what happened. An unhelpful result is worth recording too.
Lesson complete.

Lesson 6
Make time for contact
Man is by nature a social animal.
Aristotle
Part 1
Time alone
Being alone can be pleasant. Spending every evening avoiding messages and watching porn may feel different. Look at how your time alone is going before deciding that you need more of it or less.

items.t: Talking to a stranger would be less pleasant
Talking was more positive, on average

atoms.t: In experiments by Nicholas Epley and Juliana Schroeder, train and bus commuters were asked to speak with a stranger, keep to themselves, or travel as usual.
Those assigned to speak reported a more positive experience on average than those assigned to stay alone. People making predictions had expected the opposite.
The finding doesn’t promise that every conversation will go well. It suggests that an awkward prediction can sometimes be less accurate than a respectful attempt.
Part 2
A small attempt
A small attempt is enough today. Ask someone about their week. Suggest a short call. Invite a friend to do something at a particular time.
“Want to play on Thursday evening?” is easier to answer than “We should hang out sometime.”
You don’t have to explain your porn use. An ordinary conversation can give an isolated evening some company.

If you want support with recovery, ask separately and say what would help: listening for ten minutes, joining you for a walk, or helping you find a clinician. Let the person decide what they can offer.
Part 3
While you wait
Have something else to do if they’re busy. Sending an invitation and staring at the phone all evening can make the attempt feel much more loaded than it needs to be.
Leave room for a reply and carry on with your plans. Silence alone doesn’t tell you what the other person thinks of you.
If you have no safe person to contact, check a class, club, community group, or suitable support service. Find out how to attend and what it costs.
A regular meeting gives you another chance to see the same people. Friendship usually needs time and effort from both sides. Today, your part is to make one reasonable beginning.
What brings no benefit to the hive brings none to the bee.
Marcus Aurelius
Today’s task
Make time for contact
Call someone, send a specific invitation, or spend time in a conversation or shared activity. Choose contact that’s safe and appropriate.
If no personal contact is available, check how to join a regular group or access a suitable service.
Save one option under Support. After an unanswered invitation, leave room for a reply and continue another activity.
You’ve taken a contact step or checked a group or service you can access. You don’t need a reply to finish.

Lesson 7
Review the first week
It is not that we have a short time to live, but that we waste much of it.
Seneca
Part 1
What made a difference
This week gave you several things to try. The useful question now is which of them made a difference in your actual evenings. You don’t need to make the answer encouraging.
Suppose the phone stayed across the room on two nights. On the third, you brought it back because you couldn’t hear the alarm. “I have no discipline” misses a detail you can fix.
A louder alarm or a different shelf might help. But “moving the phone solved everything” also says more than three nights can show.
Look at what happened after each change. Did you leave the phone where you put it? Did you stop browsing when you planned?
Could you start the activity you had ready? If something helped, name the part that helped. If it didn’t, name what got in the way.
Part 2
Quiet nights and hard ones
There’s a difference between preparing something and using it during an urge. A quiet night can show that the phone’s new charging place is convenient.
It can’t yet tell you how you’ll respond on a harder night. Write what you know and leave the rest open. That will make the next decision easier.
Review the sleep plan from Day 4 too. Was the stopping time realistic? Did work run late? Did the quieter activity help you stay out of the feed?
Keep what fitted your life and change one thing that didn’t. Several changes at once can make it hard to tell what mattered.
Part 3
Next week
If nothing helped clearly, choose one small change to try next week. If the problem still seriously affects your life, use the support contact you saved. Help doesn’t have to wait until Day 84.
Then do something you enjoy. Have a meal, watch a film, play a game, or spend time with someone. A slip this week doesn’t take that away.
The course should help you spend more time living your life, including the parts that don’t need a lesson attached to them.
Question
Which change helped you most this week?
Choose one.

Lesson 8
Measure more than a streak
Not everything that can be counted counts, and not everything that counts can be counted.
William Bruce Cameron
Part 1
What a streak leaves out
A streak tells you how many days in a row you’ve kept a rule. That can be encouraging. But it leaves out a lot of what happens in those days.

items.t: Argues with the urge in bed until exhausted
Puts the phone away earlier and gets back to the evening

atoms.t: Imagine two people who haven’t watched porn for two weeks. One spends every night in bed arguing with the urge until they’re exhausted.
The other puts the phone away earlier and gets back to a game, a conversation, or sleep. The counters match. Their evenings don’t.
Part 2
One more measure

Researchers led by Benjamin Harkin reviewed 138 experiments on monitoring progress towards different goals. Monitoring helped goal achievement on average, though the studies covered many kinds of goals and weren’t a test of this course.
The point for you is to record something that helps you make a decision, rather than record more for its own sake.
Choose one measure beyond the streak. You might note how much time watching took, whether the phone stayed out of bed, or whether you used the steps you planned when an urge appeared.
Keep it brief. If the number is unknown, write “unknown.” A guess dressed up as a measurement won’t help later.
Part 3
What the record is for
After a slip, the earlier nights still happened. The charger you moved is still there.
The activity you enjoyed is still available. A counter restarting doesn’t erase those things. Look at what you can use again today.
Results can also be mixed. Perhaps you’re watching less but staying up late on another feed. Perhaps urges remain strong, but you’re ending searches sooner.
Those differences matter because they point to different next steps. Sleep needs attention in the first example; remembering to act earlier may matter in the second.
Check your notes when you need to decide what to keep or change. If logging starts taking over the day or making you repeatedly check yourself, simplify it.
A few useful facts are enough. The record should help you understand an evening, then let you get on with it.
Measure what is measurable, and make measurable what is not so.
Galileo Galilei
Today’s task
Measure more than a streak
Choose one measure besides a streak: time spent watching, nights with the phone out of bed, or whether you used your response to an urge.
Record what you know about the last seven days, with unknown for gaps. Then repeat one useful action today, or try a small version if you’re still finding what helps.
The measure and starting information are saved, and you’ve tried one action.

Lesson 9
Stop sooner after a slip
Our greatest glory is not in never falling, but in rising every time we fall.
Often attributed to Confucius
Part 1
The next hour
You’ve watched porn after deciding not to. The next thought may be, “The streak is gone, so I might as well carry on.” That thought can turn a short episode into a lost night.
The next hour still has something in it. You might sleep, eat, keep an appointment, or finish a task.
Closing the screen now keeps more of those things possible. You can look at why you watched later, when you’re less tired and the content is closed.
Part 2
The first half-hour
Think about what usually happens in the first half-hour after a slip. Do you keep searching? Start insulting yourself? Cancel plans?
Stay awake reading advice? One of those actions may be adding more trouble than the first decision did. Choose where you’ll stop that part next time.

steps: Leave the phone on the shelf

atoms.t: For a late-night episode, the steps could be simple: close the content, leave the phone on the shelf, wash, and get ready for bed.
For an afternoon, you might put the laptop away and make lunch. Write steps that fit the hour. A long walk isn’t helpful as your only answer if you can’t leave home at midnight.
Ending an episode doesn’t mean pretending it had no consequences. If you missed work or broke an agreement, that may need attention.
Deal with the immediate problem first, then choose a specific repair or ask for help. Repeating “I’m terrible” doesn’t tell you how to do either.
Part 3
Keep it short
Use a recent example if you have one. If you haven’t slipped, prepare the steps for a possible future episode. There is no reason to create a mistake so you can practise recovering from it.
Keep the note short enough to read when you’re upset. Put the first action at the top.
The purpose is to help you stop sooner and resume the day, without needing to feel forgiven, motivated, or certain before you begin.
A gem cannot be polished without friction, nor a man perfected without trials.
Seneca
Today’s task
Stop sooner after a slip
Add After a slip to your plan. Using a recent example if available, note what you did in the first thirty minutes.
Then write the steps you want to use: close the content, put the device in a named place, and begin the next necessary activity.
Choose the activity for the likely hour, such as food, work, or bed. If you haven’t slipped, prepare the steps for a possible episode without creating one.
The plan names the first action, device location, and what you’ll do next.

Lesson 10
Use the hours that remain
The perfect is the enemy of the good.
Voltaire
Part 1
Look at what’s left
One missed session becomes a reason to stop training. A late start becomes a reason to abandon work.
A slip becomes permission to keep watching. The original mistake gets bigger because the next decision treats the day as already lost.
Listen for the sentence that does this: “I’ll start Monday,” “There’s no point now,” or “I’ve ruined it.” Then look at what’s actually left.

At eleven at night, you can still prepare for bed. At eleven in the morning, you can still eat breakfast and begin a piece of work. The answer depends on the hour, not on making the day look perfect again.

items.t: Tomorrow starts with even less sleep
The next hour can be used differently

atoms.t: Suppose you watched for twenty minutes after a difficult shift. If you keep searching for another hour, tomorrow starts with even less sleep.
If you close it now, those twenty minutes remain a mistake, but the next hour can be used differently. That difference is worth protecting.
Part 2
Check the details
Today, try the steps you wrote yesterday while you aren’t dealing with an urge. Close a harmless tab, put the device where you planned, and move to the room or activity you chose.
Check the details. Can you hear the alarm? Is the kitchen available? Does the next activity need something you haven’t prepared?
Fix one awkward step. A plan that says “go outside” needs an indoor option if going out at night is unsafe.
A plan that says “call a friend” needs something to do if the friend is busy. The easier beginning is often more useful than stronger promises.
Part 3
Two different tests
This practice shows whether you can follow the instructions in your room.
When you use them during an urge, you’ll learn something else: whether they help you stop and move on. Keep those two observations separate.
If today is going well, let it keep going well. You can practise the steps without ruining anything first. Returning after a mistake is a skill worth preparing, not a mistake you need to manufacture.
Question
You watched late at night after deciding not to. What helps with the rest of the night?
Choose one.

Better a diamond with a flaw than a pebble without.
Confucius

Check whether it fits the hour when you usually watch. Fix one obstacle, such as an unavailable room or an unsafe late-night walk. Use an accessible option if moving isn’t possible.

Lesson 11
Try one change for a week
The path up and the path down are one and the same.
Heraclitus
Part 1
The whole week
An unusually easy evening can make you feel the problem is solved. A difficult one can make you feel nothing has changed. Neither evening tells the whole story.
Look at the last week. How much time did you spend watching? What happened when you noticed an urge? How did you respond after a slip or a missed task?
Compare that with the starting notes you wrote on Day 1. Keep the comparison as specific as the notes allow.

head: What happens
What it needs
rows: You notice sooner, but can’t put the phone down
You notice only half an hour into searching

atoms.t: Part 2
Different problems
For example, you might be noticing the urge sooner but still struggling to put the phone down. That’s different from not noticing until you’ve been searching for half an hour.
The first problem needs help with beginning the next action. The second needs a clearer warning sign, such as opening a particular account.
You might also be watching less while still losing sleep to unrelated videos. That is a mixed result, and it deserves to stay mixed in the record.
Praising the reduction while ignoring the lost sleep would leave you with the wrong next task.
Part 3
One change for seven days

If the starting notes are thin, say so. “I used to watch most nights, but I didn’t record the time” is enough. You can start a clearer note now. You don’t need to reconstruct every old evening from memory.
Choose one change to try for seven days. Maybe the evening activity needs an easier beginning, the browsing needs an earlier ending, or the charger needs a different place.
Change the detail that actually got in the way. Doing five new things at once makes the result harder to understand and gives you more to remember.
Put a Day 18 reminder in your notes or calendar. When it arrives, ask whether you tried the change and what happened.
If the situation never came up, you won’t have an answer yet. Wait until it does. Seven days gives you a time to check, not a reason to declare a result you haven’t seen.
Nothing endures but change.
Heraclitus
Today’s task
Try one change for a week

Choose one change for the next seven days. Prepare it today and save a Day 18 review reminder. Write what you want to learn from trying it.
The comparison is written, the change is ready, and the review reminder is saved.

Lesson 12
Repeat one useful action
Character is simply habit long continued.
Plutarch

items.t: “I keep watching longer than I intend.”

items.l: Claims to be everything you are
items.t: “I’m hopeless.”

atoms.t: Part 1
Something you do
“I keep watching longer than I intend” describes something you do. “I’m hopeless” claims to describe everything you are.
The first sentence gives you a problem to work on. The second makes the next attempt seem pointless.
You might prefer a more encouraging description, such as “I’m someone who takes care of my time.” If it helps, use it. But give it an action.
Put the phone away after brushing your teeth, or begin a short piece of work before opening a feed. Then you’ll know what keeping the commitment looks like.
Part 2
No fixed number of days
Phillippa Lally and her colleagues followed people repeating everyday behaviours over twelve weeks. The behaviours became more automatic at different speeds for different people.
Their findings don’t support a fixed number of days in which everybody forms a habit. A missed repetition is a reason to look at what happened, not proof that you’ve missed a universal deadline.
Consider someone who plans to read after dinner. On three nights they do. On a fourth, dinner happens elsewhere and the book is at home.
“I’m not a reader after all” explains nothing useful. Keeping the book in their bag might. Or they may choose a different cue on nights out.
Do the same with your commitment. If you forgot, choose a reminder you will see. If the action took too much effort, make the beginning smaller.
If the event you linked it to didn’t happen, decide how to handle that day. Those answers are easier to use than a verdict about your character.
Part 3
One behaviour this week
Choose one behaviour for the next week and set a Day 19 reminder. You can keep the change from yesterday instead of adding another. Repeating one action is enough work if that action matters.
The notes can stay simple: did it happen, and what got in the way? Over time, they may give you reasons to trust the commitment.
You won’t need to argue yourself into believing a larger claim about who you’ve become.
How long are you going to wait before you demand the best for yourself?
Epictetus
Today’s task
Repeat one useful action
Choose one behaviour to repeat for a week. You can keep the Day 11 change. Write the cue and action, such as putting the phone away after brushing your teeth.
Prepare what it needs and try it when the cue occurs. If it hasn’t occurred, name the first expected chance. Record missed attempts honestly and set a Day 19 review.
The behaviour, first chance, setup, and review are clear.
Lesson complete.

Lesson 13
Choose your own reason
He who knows others is wise; he who knows himself is enlightened.
Lao Tzu
Part 1
Your reason

Why do you want to change your porn use? Your answer might be sleep, time, a relationship agreement, faith, or difficulty stopping when you want to. Start there. You don’t need to borrow somebody else’s reason.
Beatrice, whose smoking story is published by the CDC, described how a letter from her son helped her decide to quit. She also used medication and support from people around her.
She had a personal reason to quit, alongside practical help. It doesn’t show that caring about someone is enough by itself, or that smoking treatment should be copied into this course.

items.t: “I want to stop losing sleep.”
“I need to become a better person.”

atoms.t: Part 2
Words you’d recognise
Give your own reason a sentence you could recognise on a tired evening. “I want to stop losing sleep” is clearer than “I need to become a better person.”
“I want to keep the agreement we made” points to a commitment you can discuss and follow. The wording doesn’t have to sound inspiring.
Guilt alone doesn’t tell you how severe the problem is. Moral disapproval by itself does not establish compulsive sexual behaviour disorder.

A personal or religious choice can still matter to you without being a diagnosis. If you have persistent difficulty controlling sexual behaviour and daily life is seriously affected, seek qualified assessment.
Ask whether the reason has turned into an insult. “I regret breaking our agreement” names a decision.
“I’m disgusting” attacks the whole person and leaves the agreement untouched. Bring the sentence back to what you want to do, protect, or repair.
Part 3
Act on it
Then give the reason some time today. If sleep matters, end browsing when you planned. If a relationship matters, give the person your attention or discuss the agreement honestly.
If faith matters, make time for a practice you freely choose. The action should follow your reason, rather than serve as punishment.

You may still be unsure. Keep the rule about your behaviour clear while you think. You can choose to stop watching without inventing damage, illness, or a dramatic explanation for why the choice matters.

Lesson 14
Return after a missed day
Difficulties strengthen the mind, as labour does the body.

Part 1
When the newness wears off
The newness wears off. The charger is in its new place, the lessons are familiar, and the first burst of motivation has passed. That is when a small routine needs to be easy enough to keep.
Choose how you’ll return after a missed day. Open the next lesson when you have time, do one useful action, and continue.
You don’t owe the course several extra lessons because yesterday was busy. Turning a missed day into a debt can make coming back feel much harder.
Suppose you miss two days while travelling. When you get home, you could restart Day 1 and announce a stricter plan.
Or you could put the phone back on its charging shelf and resume where you stopped. The second choice uses something you already prepared. You can improve it later if travel exposed a problem.
Part 2
Slips and low motivation

Keep a different answer ready for a slip. Use the steps in “After a slip,” then return to the next thing the day needs. Reading more isn’t always the next useful action. Late at night, sleep may matter more.
Low motivation also deserves a specific answer. Which part has been helping enough to keep? Perhaps the phone stays out of bed even on days you don’t feel like doing a lesson.
Keep that. If an exercise repeatedly doesn’t fit, change it instead of forcing another attempt for the sake of finishing.
Continuing also includes noticing when more help is needed.
If the course is making you more distressed, or control and daily life are getting worse, talk to a qualified professional. Repetition isn’t a reason to ignore that information.

Lesson 15
What to do when an urge starts
No state is so bitter that a calm mind cannot find in it some consolation.
Seneca
Part 1
Before the reach
An urge can feel like a decision you’ve already made. You notice the familiar thought, reach for the phone, and start searching. The few seconds before that reach are worth paying attention to.
Try describing what happens without finishing the story for it. “I want to open that account” tells you more than “I’m going to relapse.”
The first sentence leaves room to put the phone down. The second can make watching feel inevitable.

atoms.cap: You can act before the urge fades. It may come with you for a while.

atoms.t: Part 2
You don’t have to wait
Urges don’t follow a timetable. Some ease quickly; others return or stay uncomfortable. You don’t have to wait for the feeling to disappear before changing what you do.
Close the content, move the device, and begin the next activity you chose. The urge may come with you for a while.
Suppose you’re in bed and remember a video. The memory itself hasn’t broken your rule. Searching for it would be the next action.
Put the phone on the shelf and get ready for sleep. If you need another step, sit somewhere else briefly or read a few pages. Choose something you can actually do at that hour.
Part 3
The earliest sign
Look for the earliest sign you usually recognise. It might be opening a feed, switching to private browsing, or thinking “just a quick look.”
You needn’t catch the very first thought. Catching the sequence sooner than usual is still useful.
Write one sentence for that moment: “When I open that account, I’ll close it and put the phone on the kitchen counter.”
Keep the beginning specific. “Be strong” leaves you with another decision to make while you’re already tempted.
If no urge happens today, prepare the steps and practise putting the device away. Don’t search for material to test them. You can find out whether the steps help when an urge appears on its own.
You have power over your mind, not outside events. Realize this, and you will find strength.
Marcus Aurelius

Part 1
Start with the facts
What was happening before you wanted porn? Sometimes the answer is sexual desire.
Sometimes you’re tired, annoyed, avoiding work, or filling an empty evening. There may be several things going on, or no clear explanation.
Start with the facts. You came home late. You hadn’t eaten. A task was waiting. You opened the phone while sitting on the bed.
Those details give you more to work with than a theory about what every urge must mean.

An action that fits
The next action should fit what you can identify. Hunger calls for food. A difficult email may need a first sentence or a request for help.
Wanting company may call for an invitation, with something else to do while you wait. None of those steps guarantees the urge will disappear. They deal with a problem that was there before it.
Imagine someone coming home after an argument. Watching might postpone the conversation for an hour, but the disagreement will still need attention.
Tonight they could stop browsing, eat, and decide when to speak again. Trying to solve the whole relationship while upset is a much larger task.

You also don’t need a hidden emotional explanation for every sexual feeling. If desire is the main thing you notice, keep the porn rule clear and decide separately how you want to handle masturbation or intimacy.
Another person’s interest and consent matter; sex isn’t a task somebody else owes you.

Today, name one likely need and one action that fits it. If you’re unsure, write “unsure” and use the simple steps you’ve already prepared. Analysis can wait until you’ve closed the content.
Later, check what happened. Perhaps lunch helped with hunger but didn’t change the urge. That’s useful information. You met one need and still had to choose what to do with the feeling.

Lesson 17
Close the screen and move
Walking is man’s best medicine.
Hippocrates, traditionally attributed
Part 1
Move before you’ve decided
You don’t always have to settle the argument in your head before standing up. Closing the laptop and moving to the kitchen can happen while part of you still wants to keep watching.
Movement helps here because it interrupts what you’re doing. The new room gives you a chance to start something else.
It isn’t a guaranteed way to remove an urge, and it doesn’t need to be strenuous. Standing, wheeling to another space, or putting the device out of reach may be enough to change the next action.
Part 2
Rehearse where it happens
Think about where urges usually happen. If it’s the sofa after work, rehearse from the sofa. Put the phone down, get up, and go where you planned.
Find the awkward detail now. Are your shoes elsewhere? Is the kitchen occupied? Does the next activity require a device you’ve just put away?
Fix the beginning rather than making the promise bigger. Keep a book beside the chair. Prepare a drink. Choose an indoor activity when going out isn’t possible.
If leaving the room would be unsafe or inaccessible, close the content and change the position of the device instead.
Part 3
When the urge arrives
When an urge arrives, use the first step before negotiating how long you might watch.
You can still feel tempted while making tea or opening your coursework. Give the next activity a few minutes before deciding whether to change it.
Today, try the steps once without an urge. That checks whether the instructions fit your home and circumstances.
It doesn’t establish that they’ll work every time you’re tempted. After actual use, record whether you stopped watching and what helped or got in the way.
If moving rooms repeatedly leaves you opening the same material elsewhere, change what happens after the move. The room was only the beginning. You still need something to do there.
Action is the antidote to despair.
Joan Baez

The soul becomes dyed with the colour of its thoughts.
Marcus Aurelius
Part 1
The first minute
Changing what you do works best when you’ve prepared the first minute. “Find something else” is hard to follow when the phone is already in your hand.
Look back at the change you chose on Day 11. Did you try it? Did the situation happen? What made it easier or harder?

atoms.t: Part 2
When the beginning isn’t ready
Suppose you planned to cook after work instead of browsing in bed. On Tuesday you had ingredients and began. On Thursday you were hungry, the fridge was empty, and you reached for the phone.
The useful change may be keeping an easy meal available. Cooking wasn’t necessarily the wrong choice; its beginning wasn’t ready.
Other addictions offer practical examples of preparation. GamCare’s gambling guidance includes tools such as self-exclusion and planning for difficult situations.
These approaches address access and decisions in advance. They don’t show that gambling and porn use have the same causes or need the same treatment.

Your next difficult hour
For your next difficult hour, choose an activity that fits the need you noticed. Prepare what it takes to begin. If it’s company, make an invitation and have another activity ready while you wait.
If it’s rest, avoid replacing browsing with a demanding workout. If it’s a delayed task, choose the first manageable part.
You can keep the change from Day 11 when it’s helping. You don’t need a new technique because the calendar has reached a new lesson.
If it failed, change one detail and check it after you’ve had a chance to use it.

An alternative may feel less immediately appealing than porn. It can still be worth doing. Judge whether it helped you stop and use the time as you intended, rather than whether it produced the same feeling.

The body should be treated more rigorously, that it may not be disobedient to the mind.

Part 1
A short checklist
HALT is a reminder to check whether you’re hungry, angry, lonely, or tired. It’s a short checklist, not an explanation for every urge.

A safe contact or a shared activity

atoms.t: The check should lead somewhere simple. If you haven’t eaten, get food. If you’re tired, prepare for the next sleep period.
If you’re angry, step away from the argument before deciding what to say. If you’re lonely, consider a safe contact or a shared activity. Several answers can fit at once.
There will also be times when none fits. You may be rested, fed, and still want porn. Use the steps you’ve prepared instead of forcing the feeling into one of four boxes.
Sexual desire doesn’t need to be renamed hunger or loneliness before you can choose what to do.

Review your behaviour

If it was too much for the evening, shorten the beginning. If the cue didn’t occur, wait for a real chance before judging the habit.
Consider a late shift. You might have planned to go running after work, then arrive home hungry and exhausted.
Eating and going to bed could be the better decision that night. Keeping the larger goal doesn’t require treating every tired evening as a test of character.

Separate questions
For today’s practice, choose the next action from the facts in front of you. Make it small enough to begin now.
Close the triggering material first; checking how you feel while continuing to browse leaves the main action unchanged.
Afterwards, note whether the basic need was met and whether you kept the porn boundary. Those are separate questions.
A meal can help with hunger even if the urge remains. You can continue choosing your actions while it does.

Lesson 20
Notice an urge without acting on it
You can’t stop the waves, but you can learn to surf.
Jon Kabat-Zinn
Part 1
What urge surfing is

Urge surfing means noticing an urge without immediately acting on it. The name can sound more complicated than the exercise. You’re making room for a feeling while keeping your hands off the search button.

items.t: No clear drop in the mindfulness group
Fewer in the mindfulness group

atoms.t: In a study of 123 student smokers, Sarah Bowen and Alan Marlatt tested brief mindfulness instructions. Reported urges didn’t clearly fall more in the mindfulness group, but that group reported fewer cigarettes over the following week.
It was a short smoking study, not proof about this course. It does illustrate why feeling less craving and smoking less are different outcomes.
Part 2
How to try it
If you’d like to try the exercise, close the content first. Sit or stand somewhere comfortable and notice what’s present: a thought, restlessness, tightness, or the wish to reach for the phone.
You don’t have to find a bodily sensation. Breathe normally and let the feeling be there for a minute or two without searching.
Then begin the next thing you’ve chosen. Put the phone away, make food, return to work, or prepare for bed. The exercise needs that ending.
Watching the feeling indefinitely can turn a short pause into another long evening spent thinking about porn.
If paying attention to sensations makes you more distressed or absorbed in the urge, stop.
Use a different response, such as changing rooms or asking for support. This is an option, not a requirement to sit through escalating discomfort.
Part 3
What to record

You can practise the steps when you aren’t tempted. That teaches you how to do them, but won’t tell you yet whether they help during an urge. Don’t deliberately expose yourself to content to find out.
When you do use the exercise, record the next action. Did you close the content and move on?
The urge may have eased, stayed, or returned. Keep that detail honest without making disappearance the condition for success.

The nearer a man comes to a calm mind, the closer he is to strength.
Marcus Aurelius

Lesson 21
Make a separate choice about masturbation
Nothing in excess.
Delphic maxim
Part 1
Two separate choices
Porn and masturbation are separate behaviours. A course about changing porn use should make that distinction clear.
For some people, masturbation without porn fits the change they want. For others, it repeatedly leads to searching or becomes difficult to stop.
Some prefer abstinence for personal reasons. Choose a rule you can describe and later review, rather than assume one answer suits everyone.
Look at what actually happens. Can you keep the device away? Do you start searching afterwards?
Are you choosing freely, or spending more time than you intended and missing things that matter? These questions give you something to assess without declaring ordinary desire a disease.
Part 2
A rule you can review
You might choose, for now, not to use porn and not to take the phone into a private place where you usually search.
You might also decide to pause masturbation while you work out a recurring problem. State the rule plainly and set a time to reconsider it on Day 35.
Avoid turning the review into a hunt for danger in every thought. Attraction, a dream, or an unwanted memory isn’t an action crossing your boundary.
If an explicit image appears accidentally, close or move past it. The decision after exposure matters more than finding a label for the exposure itself.
Part 3
Partners and your own rule
If you have a partner, any change involving them needs discussion and consent. Sex isn’t an emergency replacement for porn, and a partner isn’t responsible for making your urges disappear.
A rule about your own viewing can be followed even when someone else isn’t available or interested.
Today, write the boundary in one or two sentences. Prepare the device or room if that makes following it easier. On Day 35, look at what happened and decide whether to keep or change the rule.
If control remains difficult and life is seriously affected, ask for qualified help. You don’t need to settle every sexual decision alone before making that request.
The first and best victory is to conquer self.
Plato

Lesson 22
Understand what starts the habit
Nature does nothing in vain.
Aristotle
Part 1
More than a pleasure tank
Dopamine helps with learning and motivation. It isn’t simply a tank of pleasure that porn drains and abstinence refills.
Neuroscientist Joshua Berke’s review describes several roles for dopamine, including how it relates to reward and the effort to pursue it.
The everyday lesson is easier to follow than a brain story. When a familiar activity repeatedly gives you something you want, reminders of it can prompt you to begin.
The phone, the account, and the hour may become part of that habit.
Part 2
Wanting isn’t enjoying
Wanting also isn’t the same as enjoying. You might keep searching while feeling bored or disappointed.
Ask what you’re doing and what it’s giving you now, rather than assuming the intensity of the urge proves the activity will be satisfying.

Closing it may feel difficult even though the last few minutes haven’t been pleasant. That discrepancy is useful to notice.
Part 3
Change one reminder
Today, choose one reminder you can change before the difficult hour: the phone beside the bed, a saved account, or the moment you open a feed after work.
Keep the change specific. You can’t make every cue disappear, but you can stop leaving the easiest one ready.
Then prepare another use for the time. A walk, meal, conversation, or hobby has its own value. It doesn’t need to provide an equivalent burst of stimulation to deserve a place in your day.
Save a brief note for Day 28: what you changed, whether you used the change, and what happened.
You won’t need to claim that your brain has reset. What matters here is whether the evening became easier to spend as you intended.

We are what we repeatedly do.
Will Durant, summarising Aristotle

Lesson 23
Decide before the difficult hour
The mind is not a vessel to be filled, but a fire to be kindled.
Plutarch
Part 1
Decide in advance

Planning ahead helps because it removes a decision you would otherwise have to make while tired or tempted. You can choose where the phone goes before you’re in bed arguing about another five minutes.

rows: I open that account after dinner
I’ll close it and put the phone on the shelf

atoms.t: One form is an if then plan: “If I open that account after dinner, I’ll close it and put the phone on the shelf.” The cue is something you can recognise. The response begins with an action you can perform.
Part 2
Plans that fit

Gollwitzer and Brandstätter studied plans that specify when and where to act. In a holiday report-writing task, those who made plans were more likely to finish among participants who returned the follow-up.
Some original participants didn’t return it. The finding supports taking planning seriously; it doesn’t guarantee that a sentence will solve a difficult habit.
The plan still needs to fit the room. “I’ll call a friend” leaves you waiting if they’re busy.
“I’ll put the phone away, make tea, and send an invitation tomorrow” includes something you control now. A useful first step doesn’t depend on getting an immediate reply.
Part 3
Write and test one
Write one plan for the point where you usually start. Avoid “Whenever I feel bad, I’ll do something healthy.”
Neither half tells you exactly what to notice or begin. Opening an account, getting into bed, or finishing dinner is easier to recognise.
Try the steps once without an urge. Put the device away and begin the next activity. If you need materials, get them ready. If the action is too long, shorten the beginning.
When the cue next happens, follow the plan and see what gets in the way. Forgetting means you may need a visible reminder.
Following it but returning to porn means the next activity or support may need attention. Those are different problems, and the notes can help you tell them apart.
Forethought we may have, undoubtedly, but not foresight.
Napoleon Bonaparte

Lesson 24
Make room for food and sleep
If you would make a man happy, add not to his riches but take away from his desires.
Epicurus
Part 1
Basic care
Hunger and tiredness can make an evening harder to manage. They also deserve attention in their own right. You don’t need to prove that every urge came from them before eating or going to bed.
Look at the hours you usually struggle. Have you missed a meal? Are you staying awake after you intended to sleep?
Would the action you planned take more energy than you have? A demanding workout at midnight may make less sense than food, washing, and bed.
Part 2
Protect a realistic sleep
The sleep study on Day 4 found that repeated short sleep reduced attention even when people’s ratings of sleepiness didn’t fully reflect the decline.

Feeling that you can manage another hour awake isn’t a reliable reason to keep postponing sleep. That finding doesn’t explain every lapse in judgement, but it gives you a reason to protect a realistic sleep period.
Prepare for the actual constraints. If you work late, keep an easy meal available. If you’re caring for someone, choose the rest you can get rather than a schedule you can’t follow.
If a phone must remain nearby for calls or accessibility, keep those functions and put unrelated browsing out of the way.

Enjoying or searching?

Part 1
The visible problem

Sometimes the thing you’re avoiding is easy to name. The letter is unopened, the application unfinished, or the conversation postponed. Looking for a hidden reason can delay dealing with the visible one.

Masicampo and Baumeister ran experiments on unfinished goals and attention. Making specific plans could reduce some of the interference associated with unfinished tasks.

Part 1
No empty tank
An evening can be harder after poor sleep, stress, or a long shift. That doesn’t mean you have a fixed supply of willpower that has run empty.

The idea that self-control becomes depleted like fuel has been debated in research. A large, preregistered replication across 23 laboratories did not find convincing support for the predicted effect using its tested procedure.
That result doesn’t mean tiredness and stress have no effect. It means the simple empty-tank explanation isn’t secure enough to treat as a rule.
Part 2

Work with what you can observe. After a late shift, a complicated evening plan may be too much.
Put the phone away, eat something easy, and prepare for sleep. You can make the action smaller without deciding that further choice is impossible.
Prepare that smaller version ahead of time. If your usual hobby session takes an hour, decide what its first five minutes look like.
If cooking is too demanding, keep an easy meal available. If going outside isn’t possible, choose an indoor response.
You don’t have to turn a tired evening into a test. Close the content when you notice the search and use the simplest next action.
The urge may remain, but the whole plan doesn’t depend on winning a long argument with it.

Today’s question is practical: what can you remove from the decision?
A prepared meal, a visible reminder, or a book beside the chair can make the beginning easier. “Have more willpower” doesn’t specify a change.

Try the smaller version once, even if you’re feeling well. You’ll see whether anything is missing before you need it. After use on a difficult day, note whether it helped and what still needs attention.
If reduced expectations repeatedly leave serious problems untouched, seek more support. Keeping one night manageable is useful; it doesn’t replace help for ongoing loss of control or major distress.

Lesson 37
Practise the response
We are what we repeatedly do.
Will Durant, summarising Aristotle
Part 1
Rehearse where it starts
Practise the response you want to remember. You don’t need an urge to check where the phone goes or how the next activity begins.
Choose one plan you’ve already written. Start where the habit normally starts: the chair, the bed, or the desk.
Close a harmless tab, move the device as planned, and begin the next action. This checks the steps in the place you’ll need them.
Notice the small obstacles. The book is elsewhere. The phone needs to remain available for calls. The activity is too noisy at night.
Change the plan so it fits. Repeating an instruction that can’t be followed won’t make it more practical.
Part 2
Keep it short
If you choose the urge-surfing exercise, practise the exercise itself: notice what is present, breathe normally for a brief pause, then begin the next activity.
Simply opening its page won’t show whether you know the steps. You don’t need to create a bodily sensation or urge.

Keep practice short. The purpose is to make the beginning familiar enough to try later, not spend the evening rehearsing every possible difficulty. One attempt and one adjustment are plenty for today.
Part 3
Practice and real use
When an urge next appears naturally, use the plan. Record whether it helped you stop and move on.
That is different information from checking whether the book and charger were ready. Preparation matters, but a comfortable rehearsal can’t establish the result during an urge.
There may be no opportunity today. Leave the steps ready and go on with another activity. Searching for triggering content would turn preparation into a different exercise with an unnecessary risk.
If the plan repeatedly fails at the same point, examine that point. Perhaps the first step is too late, the alternative doesn’t fit the hour, or you need more help.
Practice should make those details visible rather than hide them behind another promise.
Excellence is an art won by training and habituation.
Will Durant, summarising Aristotle

Practise one response from the place where you usually begin browsing. Close a harmless tab, put the device away, and begin the next action. If you choose an urge exercise, practise its steps and ending too.
Fix one awkward detail. Leave the steps ready for the next naturally occurring urge, and record that result later.
You’ve practised the response and saved an adjustment if needed. No urge or triggering material is required.

Lesson 38
Keep rules that serve a purpose
No man is more unhappy than he who never faces adversity.
Seneca
Part 1
Not the harshest rule
Discipline isn’t proved by choosing the harshest rule. A rule should help you do something useful and be clear enough to follow.
The marshmallow experiments are often told as a story about children with strong or weak willpower. Later work complicates that account.
Celeste Kidd and colleagues found, in a small experiment of 28 children, that an adult’s earlier reliability affected how long children waited.
Another study by Tyler Watts and colleagues found that associations between waiting and later outcomes became much smaller after accounting for background factors and earlier abilities.
Those findings aren’t lessons about porn treatment. They are a reason to be cautious about using one difficult choice as a verdict on someone’s character. Circumstances and expectations matter too.
Part 2
What is the rule for?
Look at your own rules. Does the rule protect sleep, time, or an agreement you value? Can you tell when you’ve kept it?
Does it still make sense on a difficult day? If its purpose is mainly to hurt or shame you, reconsider it.

items.t: Putting the phone away at bedtime
Missing meals after a slip

atoms.t: For example, putting the phone away at bedtime has a clear connection to late-night browsing.
Missing meals after a slip doesn’t. The latter removes something you need without addressing how the search began or ended.
Part 3
One useful rule
Choose one useful rule and write its reason. Keep its smallest workable version available for days with less time or energy.
Flexibility about the size of an activity can help you continue while keeping the porn boundary clear.
You may still dislike following the rule in the moment. That’s different from it being pointless. Judge it from its purpose and what happens when you use it.
Today, use or rehearse the rule once. If it has no clear benefit, change the detail or remove the optional demand. You don’t need to make the course harder to prove you take it seriously.
Nothing is so fatiguing as the eternal hanging on of an uncompleted task.
William James

If an optional rule mainly punishes you or has no clear purpose, change or remove that demand. Keep needed care. Discuss professional treatment changes with the relevant clinician.
You’ve kept or changed the rule for a clear reason and taken the fitting action.

Lesson 39
Practise the part that gets in the way
Order and simplification are the first steps toward mastery.
Thomas Mann
Part 1
Where you get stuck
Self-control involves several actions you can work on separately. You might need to notice earlier, begin a response sooner, or keep doing something else while the urge remains.

head: If you…
Work on
rows: Notice only after searching has begun
A first action that takes little thought
What you’ll do in the new room

atoms.t: Find the point that usually stops you. If you notice only after searching has begun, choose an earlier sign.
If you notice but keep bargaining, prepare a first action that takes little thought. If you move rooms and then reopen the content, work on what you’ll do in the new room.

These are different problems. Adding another reminder won’t help much when you already notice the cue but the next activity is missing. A longer explanation won’t prepare dinner or put the book within reach.
Part 2
Practise one part
Choose just one part today. For noticing, place a short reminder where the search normally begins. For beginning, practise putting the device away and standing up.
For continuing, give a suitable activity a few minutes while letting the feeling remain in the background.
Suppose you successfully put the phone on the shelf but keep returning to it because you have nothing else planned.
Prepare a short activity before the evening. You can still decide later whether you want a longer session. The first few minutes give you somewhere to begin.

Practise without deliberately provoking an urge. Check whether the action fits your space and circumstances. After you use it during an urge, record which part helped and which part remained difficult.
Part 3
What the attempt shows
Don’t ask the attempt to prove you’re a disciplined person. Ask whether you could recognise and follow a useful step. That gives you something to repeat or change.
If the problem is bigger than one missing step, add support. A qualified professional can help assess ongoing difficulty.
This lesson is a way to make a practical problem more specific; it isn’t a requirement to solve everything through repeated exercises alone.

Divide each difficulty into as many parts as is feasible and necessary to resolve it.
René Descartes

Lesson 40
Let a thought remain while you act
You don’t have to control your thoughts. You just have to stop letting them control you.
Dan Millman
Part 1
A thought can stay
A thought can stay in your head while you choose another action. “One quick look” doesn’t have to become a search just because it has appeared.

Trying never to have a particular thought can make you watch for it constantly. In Daniel Wegner’s white-bear experiments, attempts to suppress a thought were followed by more of it in a later period.
This was a laboratory task, not a universal rule about every unwanted thought. It offers a reason to try something other than repeatedly demanding that the mind stop.
Part 2
Name it, then act
Name the thought briefly: “There’s the quick-look idea again.” Then begin the response you’ve chosen.
Close the content, move the device, and start what fits the hour. You don’t need a clever phrase, and you don’t need to repeat it until you feel different.
The same applies to feelings. Desire, boredom, or disappointment can be present while you make food or prepare for bed.
Letting a feeling remain doesn’t mean agreeing to act on every suggestion that comes with it.
If noticing the thought turns into more rumination, shorten the pause and move straight to a practical action.
This isn’t an instruction to spend the evening examining your mind. Use the amount of attention that helps you act.
Part 3
Try it today
Today, try the sentence with an ordinary distracting thought, if one appears. Then return to the task you were doing. Don’t deliberately summon sexual images to practise.
Later, notice whether the thought disappeared, returned, or stayed. Also notice what you did. Keeping your boundary while still feeling tempted is a possible outcome, not a contradiction.

If intrusive thoughts or distress are consuming a lot of your day, seek appropriate help. The course can offer a brief response, but persistent difficulties deserve more than a demand to think differently.
Question
The thought is “one quick look.” What can you do next?
Choose one.

Lesson 41
Give the action a time and place
Some things are in our control and others not.
Epictetus
Part 1
When and where
Decide when and where the next action starts. “I’ll make time” leaves the decision waiting for later.
In a workplace vaccination study, employees prompted to write a date and time were more likely to get vaccinated than the control group.
The increase was about 4.2 percentage points above a control rate of 33.1 percent; a date-only prompt didn’t produce a statistically clear increase.
This was a vaccination intervention. It illustrates how a specific plan can help a task happen, without proving that planning works equally for every habit.
Part 2
Cue and first action
Use the idea for one decision you keep postponing. Write the cue, first action, and what you need ready.
“After dinner, I’ll put the phone on the shelf and read the book beside the chair” is easier to begin than “I’ll have a healthier evening.”
Choose a cue that actually happens in your day. If shift times vary, a regular event may be better than a fixed clock time.
If another person is needed, include the enquiry or invitation you can make now and another action while you wait.
Try the beginning once. Can you reach the materials? Is the place available? Does the first step still fit when you’re tired? Fix one problem rather than write a more ambitious plan.
Part 3
After you use it
You can use a commitment already in your notes. The course doesn’t require a new project every day. Repeating the same helpful action is often the point.

After actual use, record what happened. If you missed it, ask whether you forgot, lacked time, or avoided starting. Those answers suggest different changes: a reminder, a shorter action, or help with the task.
Then choose the next chance. A missed plan doesn’t need a punishment attached. It needs an honest result and a decision about what you’ll do when the cue returns.

Waste no more time arguing what a good man should be. Be one.
Marcus Aurelius

Lesson 42
Plan for a difficult day
Fall seven times, stand up eight.
Japanese proverb
Part 1
A smaller day
Prepare a smaller day before you need one. Illness, travel, poor sleep, or extra work can make the usual plan unrealistic.
Choose two or three actions that protect the most necessary things. They might be eating, keeping the phone out of bed, and preparing for sleep.
Include medication or care you already need as directed. The list should fit your circumstances, not copy somebody else’s ideal routine.
Keep the porn rule clear while shrinking optional tasks. You can do a shorter hobby session or skip extra tracking without turning the day into permission to keep watching.
If an urge happens, use the simplest response you’ve prepared.

items.t: An hour of exercise and a lesson
Phone away, an easy meal, sleep

atoms.t: Part 2
A deliberate adjustment
Suppose the normal plan includes an hour of exercise and a lesson. On a late shift, you could put the phone away, eat an easy meal, and sleep instead.
That’s a deliberate adjustment. There’s no reason to add exercise at midnight just to make the day look complete.
Review the latest activity scheduled on Day 35, if it has happened. Did you attend? Did it fit? Would a shorter session or a different time help?
If the session is still ahead, keep the check for afterwards rather than invent an answer today.
Part 3
Keep it where you’ll find it
Write the smaller plan in a few lines and put it where you’ll find it. Try one part now, or confirm that the materials are ready.
When a difficult day arrives, the plan should be easier to read than a full lesson.
After that day, return to the usual routine when it fits. You don’t owe extra work to make up for having less energy.

If difficult days have become a difficult period, seek more support and adjust the plan for that reality. A small minimum can help you get through today; it doesn’t need to carry every problem indefinitely.
Do what you can, with what you have, where you are.
Theodore Roosevelt

Plan for a difficult day

Lesson 43
Learn from a slip
There is more in us than we know.
Kurt Hahn
Part 1
Stop first, review later
After a slip, stop the episode before trying to explain it. Close the content and return to what the hour needs. Review it later, when you can look at a few facts without continuing the search.
Choose the moment where the evening changed. What happened before opening the content? Which warning sign did you notice?
What stopped you from using the response? You don’t need to reconstruct every minute or collect explicit details.
Part 2
What research suggests

Research on substance use gives one reason to examine responses after setbacks. A trial involving 286 people compared usual aftercare with therapist-led relapse prevention and mindfulness-based relapse prevention after treatment.
Outcomes differed across follow-ups, with benefits for some measures. These were structured treatment groups, not a test of a self-guided porn course.
The useful parallel is that a setback can lead to a review of the help and skills being used. It doesn’t prove the person is beyond help, and it doesn’t mean every addiction needs the same treatment.
Part 3
One obstacle, one change
Suppose you noticed the urge but the planned walk wasn’t possible because it was late and unsafe to go out. Add an indoor option.
If the response was available but you kept negotiating for another video, move the first action earlier. If neither change seems sufficient, consider professional support.
Keep the review short: the event, the obstacle, and one change. You can use a recent episode, but there’s no need to create one for this exercise.
If nothing has happened, check whether your current steps still fit.
Part 4
Use what you learn
Then do something with the information. Prepare the alternative, change the reminder, or make the enquiry. An explanation is useful when it changes the next attempt.
If the episodes remain frequent or seriously affect daily life, get qualified help. Reviewing the same evening repeatedly isn’t a reason to postpone a more useful level of support.
While there’s life, there’s hope.
Cicero
Today’s task
Learn from a slip
Review a recent slip or close call, if available. Close the content first. Later, write what happened before it, the first sign you noticed, and the obstacle to using your response.
Make one practical change or take a support step. If no example exists, check that your current after-slip steps still fit. Don’t create a mistake for the review.
The review leads to a change, a confirmed plan, or a request for help.

Lesson 44
Take care and make a repair
Experience is the name everyone gives to their mistakes.
Oscar Wilde
Part 1
Responsibility without punishment
Taking responsibility after a mistake doesn’t require treating yourself badly. Food, sleep, and appropriate care are still needed.

Breines and Chen tested brief self-compassion exercises across four experiments. Some participants showed greater motivation to improve or make amends; in one experiment, they spent more time studying after a difficult test.
These were short experimental tasks. They don’t establish a treatment for porn use, but they challenge the assumption that kindness must prevent effort.
Part 2
Describe it plainly
Describe the event without the insult. “I watched after deciding not to, and I stayed up late.”
Then name the next useful action: end browsing, prepare for sleep, or deal with a missed commitment. The factual sentence already allows responsibility.
If an agreement was broken, consider a proportionate repair. An apology or honest conversation may be needed.
Make it relevant to the person affected, rather than a demand that they reassure you or hear every detail.
Punishment can add another problem. Skipping meals after a slip leaves you hungry. A punishing workout can postpone sleep.
Calling yourself worthless may make you avoid the very people or tasks that need attention.
Part 3
Care and repair

Today, choose one act of care and one repair if a repair is needed. If there hasn’t been a recent mistake, keep the steps ready and continue with normal care. You don’t have to invent guilt to use this lesson.
You may still feel ashamed after taking the action. Feeling better isn’t the condition for eating, washing, or resuming the day. Give those things their time while the feeling settles or remains.
If shame or self-hatred is severe or persistent, ask for qualified support. A brief exercise may help with the next decision, but ongoing distress deserves attention beyond a daily lesson.
You can seek that help while continuing to work on the behaviour you want to change.

Which actions take responsibility after a slip?
Choose all that fit.

Failure is instructive. The person who really thinks learns quite as much from his failures as from his successes.
John Dewey

If there hasn’t been a mistake, keep ordinary care and prepare the steps for later. You don’t need to invent guilt or a confession.
You’ve taken care of a need and addressed a real consequence where there is one.

Lesson 45
Adjust the plan for today
Wherever there is a human being, there is an opportunity for kindness.
Seneca
Part 1
Days that ask for less
Some days ask for less. You’re ill, work runs late, sleep was poor, or several problems arrive together. The plan should account for that.
Use the smaller day you prepared on Day 42. Keep the most necessary care and the simplest steps for stopping porn.
Shorten optional activities. If an exercise doesn’t fit, postpone it without turning it into a debt.
For example, a planned hour at the gym may become a short walk or rest. A full cooking session may become an easy meal.
A lesson may wait until tomorrow. The adjustment should fit the reason the day is difficult.
Part 2
Less, not nothing
Notice when “less” quietly becomes abandoning everything. You may not have time for a hobby, but putting the phone away at bedtime could still be possible.
Choose what remains within reach rather than ask whether the entire routine can be completed.
If an urge appears, begin with the first action you control. Close the content and move the device or yourself as planned.
You can decide about the rest of the evening afterwards. Keep an indoor or accessible option for times the usual response is unavailable.
Tell someone about a practical need if that would help: a delayed deadline, an appointment, or extra support. You don’t have to disclose sexual details to ask for a meal, company, or help with work.
Part 3
Adapt one commitment
Today, adapt one commitment to the day you actually have. Record the change briefly if it will help you use it again. Otherwise, take the action and leave the notes alone.
If rough days keep repeating, reconsider the weekly plan or seek support for what’s happening.
A routine built for unusually easy days won’t become realistic through more self-criticism. Keep the useful parts and change what the circumstances require.
Be tolerant with others and strict with yourself.
Marcus Aurelius
Today’s task
Adjust the plan for today
Adapt one commitment to today’s circumstances. Shorten an activity, use the easier meal, or postpone an optional lesson while keeping necessary care and the porn response.
Use the Bad day minimum if it fits. If the day is going well, confirm the version you’d use when needed and keep today’s helpful routine.
You’ve followed a fitting version of the day or prepared it for a future difficulty.

Lesson 46
Get support during a difficult period
The sun is new each day.
Heraclitus
Part 1
Longer than a bad day
A difficult period can last longer than a bad day. Grief, illness, conflict, or sustained pressure may need a different plan and more support.
Rebecca’s smoking story, published by the CDC, describes returning to smoking during a divorce after seven months without it. Later, wanting to be there for her grandson mattered in another attempt.
Her account also includes care for depression and running. It is a personal story, not evidence that exercise cures depression or that smoking treatment should be copied here.
What it makes clear is the importance of the surrounding situation. A return to an old behaviour may happen while other difficulties are changing.
Those difficulties deserve attention as well as the behaviour itself.
Part 2
What has become harder

Ask what has become harder lately. Is sleep disrupted? Are you alone more often? Are responsibilities beyond the time or energy available? Choose one practical adjustment and one source of help if needed.
You might reduce optional course tasks, ask for help with a responsibility, or check a clinician’s availability.
Keep food, rest, and necessary care. If support is needed now, make the enquiry rather than only saving a contact for the end of the course.
Use your smaller plan for a while and give it a review date. The purpose is to see whether it fits this period, not to promise you’ll feel normal by that date. If things worsen, review sooner.
Part 3
Asking for help
Personal contact may help, but another person’s immediate reply isn’t required to complete the step. Services can be the first choice and the backup when trusted contacts aren’t available.
Today, prepare what you’ll do during the next difficult evening and how you’ll ask for help.
You can continue working on porn use without expecting one brief exercise to carry every problem that has arrived with it.

Although the world is full of suffering, it is full also of the overcoming of it.
Helen Keller
