Lesson 47
Return to the task you postponed
Sometimes even to live is an act of courage.
Seneca
Part 1
Back to Day 31
Look back at the problem you named on Day 31. Has the first step happened? If not, what made it hard to begin?
Sometimes the step was still too large. “Finish the application” may need to become “open it and find the deadline.”
Sometimes you lacked information or needed another person. Make the specific enquiry rather than keep rewriting the same intention.
A break can be useful, but give it an ending. You might walk for ten minutes and then read the letter.
If the break keeps expanding into another lost evening, prepare the first step before taking it and choose when you’ll return.
Part 2
A first sentence
Suppose an unanswered email keeps bothering you. You don’t yet know what to say, so you keep opening videos. Begin by writing the question you need answered, or a rough first sentence.
The task may still take time, but you’ve stopped asking yourself to produce the whole finished answer before starting.
Not every problem should be faced alone. A harmful relationship, unsafe workplace, or upsetting memory may require support before action.
This exercise doesn’t require confrontation, disclosure, or writing about a painful event. A safer first step can be contacting an appropriate service.
Part 3
One step today
If the Day 31 problem has been resolved, leave it resolved. Choose a current small task only if one is genuinely waiting. If no avoidance problem fits, use the time for an activity you value instead.
Today, take one step on the actual issue. Make it clear enough that you’ll know whether it happened. Save any further step with a realistic time, then let the rest of the day continue.
Dealing with a task may reduce a worry or may simply get the task moving. Either can be useful.
It doesn’t need to remove an urge to justify the effort, and an urge doesn’t need a hidden cause before you can stop watching.
The oak fought the wind and was broken, the willow bent when it must and survived.
Robert Jordan
Today’s task
Return to the task you postponed
Return to the Day 31 first step. If it hasn’t happened, make it smaller or request the information or help you need. Spend up to fifteen minutes on the safe step now.
If the issue is resolved, choose another small waiting task only if one exists. If none fits, keep a valued activity. Get support before action when safety or severe distress is involved.
You’ve taken a fitting action or made the support request. Confrontation or painful reflection isn’t required.

Lesson 48
Begin the next part of the day
The cave you fear to enter holds the treasure you seek.
Often attributed to Joseph Campbell
Part 1
The next necessary thing
The day still contains the hours that remain. A slip, a late start, or a missed task doesn’t decide what happens next.
Look at the clock and choose the next necessary thing. Late at night, that may be washing and bed.
In the afternoon, it may be lunch, an appointment, or a small piece of work. The answer should fit the hour rather than an attempt to make the record look perfect.
Use the steps you’ve already written after a slip. Close the content first. Don’t keep browsing while planning a better tomorrow. If the steps no longer fit, change one detail and begin.
Part 2
Smaller is fine
Suppose you lost an hour you wanted for study. Trying to recover it by studying deep into the night may create another cost.
You could do the most necessary ten minutes, plan the next session, and keep bedtime. The lost hour remains lost, but it doesn’t have to take tomorrow’s morning too.
Choose a smaller action when needed. Send the enquiry instead of solving the whole problem.
Prepare materials instead of completing the full session. Eat something easy instead of turning dinner into another demanding task.
Part 3
Back to the day

If the day has been going well, keep a useful commitment. There is no need to revisit every possible mistake just because the lesson concerns recovery after one. A planned activity or normal care is enough.
After taking the step, stop checking whether you’ve rescued the day. Give the meal, conversation, or rest your attention. Returning to life is easier when you let the next activity have its time.
Today’s practice is one concrete return. You don’t need to feel proud, forgiven, or fully motivated before beginning.
If serious difficulty remains, add a request for help. That can also be a practical use of the hour you still have.
Nothing diminishes anxiety faster than action.
Walter Anderson
Today’s task
Begin the next part of the day
Look at the hour and choose the next necessary activity: food, work, class, washing, or bed. After a slip, close the content and follow your saved steps first.
Begin a manageable part. If the day is going well, keep a useful existing commitment instead. Don’t add punishment to compensate for lost time.
You’ve returned to one activity that fits the hour.

Lesson 49
Take a step after a longer setback
Begin anywhere.
John Cage
Part 1
After a longer setback
A longer setback can make the future feel smaller. You may think the lost weeks or months have decided what’s possible now. Start with a decision that can still be made.
Choose one area that needs attention: work, study, health, money, or a relationship. What is the next action, and who can help with it? A first enquiry is often enough for today.
If work has fallen behind, ask about the necessary next task or deadline. If money is causing difficulty, check an appropriate advice service.
If control over porn use remains poor and life is seriously affected, seek qualified assessment. The course doesn’t need to be finished first.
Part 2
A useful beginning

Don’t promise a dramatic comeback. A useful beginning may be an appointment, a reopened assignment, or an invitation. Its size doesn’t tell you how serious the problem is. It tells you what can be done now.
Review the latest activity from Day 35 if it has occurred. Did you attend, and did it deserve the time?
If circumstances interrupted it, decide whether a shorter session or another date fits. If it’s still ahead, keep the check for afterwards.
You can maintain something already working while addressing the larger difficulty.
A meal, sleep routine, or trusted contact may remain useful even when the overall record is disappointing. Keep the value of those actions separate from the need for more help.
Part 3
Begin from here
Today, take one step and write the next only if it’s needed. If waiting for another person, choose something you can do while waiting rather than repeatedly checking for a reply.
The past may have real consequences. You don’t need to deny them to begin again. Work from the situation as it is, with whatever care, advice, or treatment it now requires.
That gives the next week a specific beginning instead of another verdict about your life.
The beginning is always today.
Mary Shelley

Lesson 50
Give an activity time before switching
The gods were bored; therefore they created human beings.
Søren Kierkegaard, paraphrased
Part 1
Jumping between clips
Boredom can send you searching for something more interesting, then keep you switching when nothing feels interesting enough. More choice doesn’t always improve the experience.

Katy Tam and Michael Inzlicht tested switching between or within videos across seven experiments involving 1,223 participants. Switching could increase boredom compared with watching without switching.
Results involving articles and some samples were less conclusive. The finding concerns those tested media tasks; it doesn’t show that every screen activity causes boredom.
Think about an evening spent jumping between clips. Each switch promises a better one.
You finish without having enjoyed much or given another activity time to become interesting. If that pattern fits, try changing the switching rather than searching harder.
Part 2
Give one activity time
Choose one activity for a short period. Reading, a game, music, a hobby, movement, or rest can all fit.
Give it enough time to begin before opening unrelated feeds. A device is fine when it’s part of the activity or needed for accessibility.
You may feel bored at first. Notice whether that changes once you’ve started. If it stays dull, the activity may be a poor fit, or you may need rest or company.
You aren’t required to call boredom good or enjoy a task because you chose it.
Part 3
What the result tells you

Use the result to decide what to keep. “Ten minutes of drawing held my attention” suggests something different from “I was too tired and wanted sleep.” Both are more useful than “I need more stimulation.”
Today, try one suitable activity without unrelated switching, then record a sentence about how it went. Don’t make the exercise another demand to avoid every screen.

If boredom is persistent alongside low mood or loss of interest in much of life, seek appropriate help. A lesson about switching is a narrow tool, and it doesn’t explain every reason an evening feels empty.

Søren Kierkegaard

Lesson 51
Choose what begins in an empty gap
Nothing is more intolerable to man than a state of complete repose.
Blaise Pascal
Part 1
The transition
The quickest activity to begin often wins the empty gap. The phone is in your hand before you’ve decided what you want from the break.
Look for the transition. Did you open a harmless feed and then start searching sexually? Did work end with no plan for the next hour?
If a particular account or search repeatedly begins the behaviour you want to stop, include it in the boundary.
Part 2
A specific rule
Keep the rule specific. “After dinner, I’ll begin the book before opening unrelated feeds” is something you can try.
“Use screens less” leaves you deciding what less means every evening. Necessary calls, work, and accessibility still need to fit.
Prepare a different beginning. Put the activity within reach, choose a short first part, and name when the break ends.
You don’t have to build a full evening schedule. One ready action can change what happens in a ten-minute gap.
Suppose you usually open a feed while waiting for food. You could keep music or a book ready for that time.
If the screen habit isn’t causing difficulty, leave it alone and work on the situation that actually matters. The course isn’t asking you to manufacture a problem with every form of leisure.
Part 3
Try it in a normal gap
Try the change during a normal gap today. If that gap doesn’t happen, prepare it for the next one. Don’t reopen triggering content to see whether you can resist.
Afterwards, ask whether the alternative was easy to begin and whether it helped you keep the boundary. If you returned to the search, look at the first point where the change stopped helping.
The useful result is a clearer beginning and ending. You can keep a harmless feed when it fits your life and change the particular habit that keeps leading somewhere you didn’t intend to go.
All of humanity’s problems stem from man’s inability to sit quietly in a room alone.
Blaise Pascal, commonly paraphrased

Choose what begins in an empty gap

Lesson 52
Try fifteen minutes without switching
Seek not that the things which happen should happen as you wish; but wish the things which happen to be as they are.
Epictetus
Part 1
Fifteen minutes
Give one slower activity a little time before deciding it isn’t enough. Some things become interesting after you’ve begun rather than in the first few seconds.
Choose fifteen minutes of reading, a hobby, a task, gentle movement, or rest. Keep unrelated feeds closed while you try it.
You can use a device when it’s part of the activity; the point is to give the activity your attention.
Suppose you begin a book and reach for a new clip after the first paragraph. Put the phone aside and read a little further before changing.
You may still decide the book isn’t for you. The difference is that you’ve given it a chance instead of comparing its opening seconds with a constantly changing feed.
Part 2
Not an endurance test
Don’t turn this into sitting still through discomfort for its own sake. If you’re exhausted, rest may be the better choice.
If the activity is inaccessible or unpleasant, adjust it. Boredom isn’t an achievement to collect.

At the end, ask what happened. Did the activity become easier to enter? Did it remain dull? Did you need a different kind of break? Keep the answer short and specific enough to choose what to do next.
If it helped, leave the materials ready for another session. If it didn’t, choose another option later. You don’t need to defend the first choice or force a daily habit from one attempt.
Part 3
A clear ending
This practice may also show how frequently you switch without thinking. You can notice a reach for the phone and return to the page without treating the reach itself as a failure.
Today, let the fifteen minutes have a clear ending. Move on to the next thing afterwards.
The exercise is a short chance to see how an activity feels when it receives attention, not a rule that every free hour must be slow, quiet, or screen-free.
Patience is bitter, but its fruit is sweet.
Often attributed to Aristotle
Today’s task
Try fifteen minutes without switching
Give one activity fifteen minutes without unrelated switching. Choose what fits: reading, a hobby, a task, gentle movement, or rest. Keep needed devices in use and unrelated feeds closed.
At the end, record whether it became easier to enter, stayed dull, or wasn’t right for the moment. Then begin the next part of the day.
You’ve tried the activity and recorded its fit. It needn’t be enjoyable or screen-free.

Lesson 53
Change one screen habit
The things you own end up owning you.
Chuck Palahniuk
Part 1
The habit causing trouble
Choose the screen habit that is actually causing trouble. Screens can support work, reading, friendship, and accessibility as well as make unwanted browsing easy.
In a small laboratory study, Anne-Marie Chang and colleagues compared prolonged evening reading on a light-emitting device with print.

The device condition affected sleep-related measures, including sleep timing. Those controlled exposures weren’t a brief phone check, so the study doesn’t justify treating every screen use as equally harmful.

For this course, begin with what you’ve observed. Is the phone in bed keeping you awake or making porn easy to reach? Is a particular feed repeatedly leading to searches? Change that use, place, or time.
Part 2
State the rule
State the rule plainly: no unrelated feeds in bed, or put the laptop away after finishing the specified work.
Keep necessary calls, alarms, care, and accessibility available. A rule that ignores those needs is likely to break for a good reason.
Use an existing rule if it’s helping. There is no need to add another boundary just to make this week’s lesson different. You can check whether the current setup still fits.
Prepare the device or room and follow the rule once when the situation occurs. If it doesn’t happen today, name when you’ll first try it. Set a Day 60 reminder to review the week.
Part 3
Review it on Day 60

At that review, ask whether you followed the rule, whether it helped, and what got in the way. A reduction in one feed that leaves you awake on another may need a different change. Keep mixed results mixed.
The aim is to make the troublesome part easier to manage while keeping the device useful. You don’t need to declare all screens bad before putting one of them away for the evening you want to have.

Lesson 54
Try an hour away from one feed
Abstinence is easier than perfect moderation.
Saint Augustine, commonly attributed
Part 1
What an hour can show
A “dopamine detox” doesn’t remove dopamine from the brain, and this course can’t promise to reset a reward system by taking away screens. Dopamine has several roles in learning and motivation.
You can still try a simpler, useful experiment: set aside one automatic feed or browsing habit for an hour and see when you reach for it.
Choose a habit that’s causing difficulty, rather than remove every enjoyable activity.
Keep necessary calls, work, care, and accessibility available. The porn boundary you chose stays in place for the whole day; this hour is about an additional habit you want to understand.
Part 2
Notice the reach

Notice the reach and what was happening. Were you waiting, avoiding a task, wanting company, or looking for a break? You might not know. Write “unsure” if so, then choose something suitable for the time.
Suppose you check the same feed every time a task becomes difficult. Closing the feed doesn’t make the task easier.
You may need to find the confusing instruction, ask a question, or take a short break with an ending. The hour can make that pattern easier to see.
Part 3
At the end of the hour
At the end, decide whether a small rule would help. Maybe the feed stays closed during the first ten minutes of work.
Maybe the existing bedtime rule is enough. If the habit isn’t causing a problem, leave it alone and review a change that’s relevant.
You may feel restless, calmer, or much the same. None of those feelings measures a brain reset. Judge the experiment from what you did and what you learned about the habit.
Today, keep the observation brief.
The purpose is to make a decision about a particular use of time, not create another system for monitoring every pleasure or repeatedly checking whether you’re recovering correctly.

Simplicity is the ultimate sophistication.
Commonly attributed to Leonardo da Vinci

Lesson 55
Prepare the first hour after waking
Lose an hour in the morning, and you will spend all day looking for it.
Richard Whately
Part 1
Decide the night before
If the first hour after waking is difficult, decide its first activity before you go to bed. You shouldn’t have to invent the morning while already scrolling.
Choose what fits: washing, breakfast, a short piece of work, a walk, or another necessary activity.
Prepare the materials. Set a realistic alarm that allows enough rest rather than use an early start as punishment.
Marcus Aurelius wrote about getting up to do the work of a human being.
You can take that as a prompt to begin a chosen responsibility, without borrowing an emperor’s schedule or making productivity the purpose of every morning.
Part 2
Fit your real schedule
Suppose you usually wake, open a feed, and search before getting out of bed.
Put the phone where you can keep needed alarm or call functions, and decide where you’ll go first. Breakfast already partly prepared can give you an easier beginning.
If you work nights, apply the idea to your waking period rather than a conventional morning.
If you’re ill or caring for someone, rest or care may be the first thing the day needs. The routine should serve the real schedule.
There may be no morning problem. Confirm what’s working and leave it alone. You don’t need to change every part of life because the course has a lesson about it.
Part 3
Check how it goes
Save a short check for the next time you wake. Did you begin the chosen activity? Was anything missing?
We’ll revisit that result tomorrow if the morning has happened; otherwise keep the reminder for afterwards.
Today, prepare one beginning or keep the routine that’s already useful. A morning plan doesn’t need many steps.
It needs something you can start, the materials to start it, and room for the amount of rest your circumstances require.
The secret of your future is hidden in your daily routine.
Often attributed to Mike Murdock

Lesson 56
Give time to something that matters
He who has a why to live can bear almost any how.
Friedrich Nietzsche
Part 1
Time for what matters
What deserves some of the time you’re trying to recover? Choose a person, activity, or responsibility with a reason that makes sense to you.
Meaning needn’t arrive as a feeling before you begin.
You can spend time with someone because the relationship matters, practise a skill because you want to learn it, or rest because your health needs it. The first session may feel ordinary.

Seneca’s first letter asks the reader to take care of time. For today’s lesson, make that practical: give something you value a place in the day, rather than spend the whole evening thinking about wasted hours.
Part 2
Make the time
Choose fifteen to thirty minutes, or a smaller block when needed. If another person or booking is involved, make the invitation or arrangement.
You can reuse the weekly activity from Day 35 instead of starting a project.
First review the latest Day 35 session and the waking routine from yesterday, if each has occurred. What did you try, and what happened?
If either is still ahead, keep its check for afterwards. If the routine didn’t fit, change one detail.
Then begin the chosen activity. Put the materials within reach, make the call, or open the first part of the task.
Give it attention for the time available. It doesn’t have to produce a dramatic sense of purpose.
Part 3
Enough as it is
When low mood or loss of interest is persistent, appropriate support may be needed.
A valued activity can be part of care without becoming a promised cure. Keep professional help available when the problem extends beyond an empty evening.
Today, record the action if it helps you plan another session. Otherwise, let the action be enough.
The point of making time is to use it, not turn every enjoyable or meaningful moment into another recovery measurement.
Life can only be understood backwards; but it must be lived forwards.
Søren Kierkegaard

Lesson 57
Arrange a shared activity
What do we live for, if it is not to make life less difficult for each other?
George Eliot
Part 1
Actual time
Give a relationship some actual time. Thinking that you should connect more won’t arrange a conversation or put a shared activity in the week.
The Harvard Study of Adult Development is often cited for the association between relationships and wellbeing.

Its long-term observations are valuable, but they don’t show that one invitation will cause better health or make porn use easy to change. Use the finding as a reason to pay attention to relationships, with realistic expectations.
Part 2
A specific invitation
Choose a person you trust or enjoy and suggest something specific: a walk on Saturday, a meal after work, or a call at a time that suits both of you.
Give them room to decline or suggest another time. Their answer isn’t a grade for the exercise.
If no safe personal contact is available, look for a regular class, group, community setting, or appropriate service you can access.
Check the time, cost, location, and how to attend. A concrete enquiry is a useful beginning.
You don’t need to disclose porn use to take part in ordinary contact. You can enjoy a meal or talk about a shared interest.
If you do want support with the problem, choose someone willing and appropriate, and explain what help you’re asking for.
Part 3
While you wait
Suppose an invitation gets no immediate reply. Send it once, then continue the evening.
Repeated checking doesn’t give the other person more time, and it can make the wait take over. Prepare another activity while the answer is unknown.
If your social life is already working, keep an existing plan and give it your attention. There’s no need to add contacts for the sake of completing a lesson.

Today, make the invitation, check attendance, or keep the shared activity. Save the details only where they’ll help you follow through. The relationship deserves time beyond its possible usefulness to recovery.
The greatest thing in the world is to know how to belong to oneself.
Michel de Montaigne

We are all so much together, but we are all dying of loneliness.
Albert Schweitzer
Part 1
Different kinds of loneliness
Loneliness can mean different things. You may have little contact, plenty of contact without closeness, or be missing one particular person. Choose a step that fits what you’re missing.
Sandstrom and Dunn studied everyday interactions with acquaintances as well as close ties.

Their findings linked more weak-tie interactions with greater wellbeing, but the observations don’t establish that brief contact cures loneliness. A familiar face can be worth greeting without carrying that much responsibility.

Lesson 59
Choose how to spend time alone
All of humanity’s problems stem from man’s inability to sit quietly in a room alone.
Blaise Pascal, adapted
Part 1
Time alone, chosen
Time alone can be restful, enjoyable, or difficult. What you choose to do with it, and whether you have other contact available, can make a difference.
Choose a short period alone deliberately instead of letting an empty gap become unplanned browsing.
Read, make something, listen to music, walk, or rest. Use a device when it’s part of the activity, with unrelated feeds closed.
Name what follows. After twenty minutes of reading, you might prepare dinner. After a quiet break, return to work or a shared activity.
A clear ending can keep a chosen pause from turning into hours you didn’t intend to lose.
Part 2
Change the setting
If being alone tends to make urges harder, choose a shared place where you can still do your own activity: a library, café, or common room if accessible.
You don’t need to speak with anyone for the change of setting to be useful.
Suppose you enjoy drawing but usually start it in bed with the phone nearby. Move the materials to the table and put the phone elsewhere.
You’re making room for the activity you chose, rather than relying on a promise to ignore a device within reach.
Part 3
Try it briefly
Try ten to twenty minutes today and notice how it went. Was it restful, absorbing, uncomfortable, or a poor fit? Record one adjustment if needed. Don’t require the time to make you calm.

If solitude brings distress that feels unmanageable, stop and choose contact or appropriate support. This is a short leisure exercise, not exposure therapy or a test of how much isolation you can tolerate.
When the time ends, begin what you named next. Keeping the ending is part of the practice.
You can learn what kind of time alone suits you without making loneliness or total screen avoidance the price of completing it.
Whosoever is delighted in solitude is either a wild beast or a god.
Aristotle

Lesson 60
Separate desire from wanting company
There is no instinct like that of the heart.
Lord Byron
Part 1
Desire or company?
Porn can offer an image of connection without providing the conversation, care, or mutual interest you may be wanting.
It can also be about sexual desire without a missing relationship behind it. Check your own situation rather than assume a single explanation.
If you want company, choose contact that fits: focused time with a willing partner or friend, an invitation, or a regular group.
If sexual desire is the main issue, look at the boundary from Day 21. You don’t need to do anything sexual to complete the lesson.

Other people’s choices
Keep other people’s choices clear. A partner isn’t responsible for preventing an urge or available whenever you feel one.
Intimacy needs mutual interest and consent. A personal rule about porn can still be followed when someone else isn’t interested or nearby.
If there’s an agreement about viewing, make sure you understand it and can discuss it honestly. Don’t expect mind-reading, and don’t use the course as a reason to demand monitoring or reassurance.

The screen review

Keep, adjust, or end that additional screen experiment from what happened. Ending an unhelpful screen experiment doesn’t automatically change your porn boundary.

One fitting step

Take one fitting step after the review. Make the contact, prepare the sexual boundary, or maintain what’s already working. You can save a group or service to try when personal contact isn’t available.
The step doesn’t need to remove desire or loneliness immediately. It should give the actual need some attention while keeping the behaviour you want to change clear.

Lesson 61
Follow up on a connection
The only way to have a friend is to be one.
Ralph Waldo Emerson
Part 1
Another meeting
Relationships usually need another meeting after the first good conversation. A reasonable follow-up gives the connection a chance to continue.
Choose someone or somewhere you already know. Suggest a specific activity, ask about the next group session, or attend again.
You don’t need to create an impressive social plan. Repeating a shared activity can be enough.

Give the other person space to choose. If they’ve declined or contact remains one-sided, stop pressing and look elsewhere. Respecting a boundary is a useful action, even when the answer disappoints you.
Part 2
Make it easy to return
If you’re returning to a group, check the details that might prevent attendance: time, transport, cost, or accessibility.
Prepare what you can. The practical beginning matters more than promising to become more outgoing.
Suppose you met someone at a class and enjoyed talking. “Would you like to get a coffee after next week’s session?” gives them something clear to answer.
A message needn’t include your full recovery story or a request for deep friendship.

When another person is busy, keep other parts of life moving. You can enjoy a hobby, make another appropriate plan, or rest while waiting. One person’s availability doesn’t decide whether the evening has value.
Part 3
One follow-up
If safe contacts are scarce, a recurring group or service may be a better starting point than trying to force closeness with someone unsuitable. Check how to join and take the first step you can.
Today, make one follow-up, attend, or register. A reply isn’t required for completion. If a clear boundary means the right action is leaving someone space, identify a different option instead.
Afterwards, remember what helped you take part and what would make returning easier. Then let the relationship be a relationship.
It doesn’t need to become another daily score or carry every difficulty you’re working through.
Friendship is a sheltering tree.
Samuel Taylor Coleridge
Today’s task
Follow up on a connection
Make one reasonable follow-up with a person or group you know. Suggest an activity, ask about the next session, register, or attend again.
If someone has declined or contact is one-sided, leave them space and choose another option. Check timing, cost, and access where needed.
You’ve followed up or attended. Respecting a clear boundary and finding another suitable option also counts.

Lesson 62
Set a safe limit on harmful contact
Associate with people who are likely to improve you.
Seneca
Part 1
Contact that makes it harder
Some contact makes the behaviour you want to change harder. A group may repeatedly send explicit material, ignore a stated limit, or pressure you to join activities you’ve chosen to stop.
Writer and former boxer Ed Latimore has described changes in his social life after stopping drinking.
His account includes how relationships fitted differently with sobriety. It’s his own account, not evidence that every friendship should end when someone changes a habit.
Part 2
A proportionate limit
Look at a specific interaction. What happens repeatedly? What limit have you chosen? Which part can you control safely?
You might mute a channel, decline an invitation, leave a conversation, or ask for support before making a larger decision.
Don’t turn a disagreement or one awkward evening into a diagnosis of the person. Describe the behaviour and choose a proportionate response.
“I won’t stay in a group that keeps sending material I’ve asked not to receive” is clearer than a broad label about bad people.
Part 3
When safety comes first
Some situations involve danger, dependence, or coercion. Get appropriate support before acting, and avoid confrontation alone when it could make you less safe.
The exercise doesn’t require leaving a home, job, or relationship today.
If there is no harmful interaction, keep or arrange time with someone you value.
You don’t need to find a bad relationship to make the lesson applicable. When personal contact is unavailable, check a suitable group or service instead.
Part 4
One safe change

Today, make one safe change or take one support step. Save the limit in your plan only if you’ll need to remember it later. Another person’s agreement isn’t required for a boundary about your own action.
The useful question is whether the contact respects the choices you’re making and the wellbeing of the people involved. Work from repeated facts, with enough help for the size of the decision.
Show me your friends, and I’ll show you your future.
Proverb
Today’s task
Set a safe limit on harmful contact
If an interaction repeatedly causes harm or ignores your limit, choose one safe change: mute a channel, limit your availability, decline an invitation, or seek support before acting.
Save your own action if you’ll need to remember it. If no harmful interaction fits, keep or arrange time with someone you value, or check a support setting when contact isn’t available.
You’ve made a safe change, taken a support step, or maintained a healthy connection. Confrontation isn’t required.

Lesson 63
Give a relationship attention
Friendship is a single soul dwelling in two bodies.
Aristotle, traditionally attributed
Part 1
Attention through action
Give a good relationship attention through something you do. Listen, help, keep a plan, make a call, or apologise where an apology is needed.
Support doesn’t have to involve discussing porn. A meal together, a shared interest, or an ordinary conversation can matter.
If you want help with the behaviour, ask clearly and check whether the person is willing and able to offer it.
Be careful about making one person your only answer. They may be busy, need limits, or lack the expertise for a serious difficulty.
Keep appropriate services available as well. A friendship and professional care can have different roles.
Part 2
Review the four sessions
Today, review the four activity opportunities scheduled on Day 35. What actually happened?
Did you attend, enjoy it, or encounter the same obstacle? Decide whether the activity deserves a continuing place or needs a change.
If some sessions are still ahead, keep their reviews for afterwards. Four dates on a calendar aren’t four completed sessions. Record what you know and leave the rest pending.
Part 3
One relationship step
Then take one relationship step. Keep an existing commitment if it’s useful.
If you send an invitation or apology, make it appropriate and allow the other person to answer in their own time. Completion doesn’t depend on a reply or forgiveness.
If no safe relationship is available, take a step towards a suitable group or service. Check attendance or contact details so the option is more than a name on a list.
Part 4
Its own value
Let the action have its own value. Helping someone isn’t a bargain that obliges them to help you later. Listening doesn’t require them to solve your problem.
The relationship can be part of a fuller week without becoming a technique you use only when an urge appears.
Keep whatever regular contact has been useful, with limits that both people can understand and respect.
The better part of one’s life consists of his friendships.
Abraham Lincoln
Today’s task
Give a relationship attention
Review the four Day 35 activity opportunities. Record what happened and whether to continue. Keep checks for any future sessions after they occur.
Then do one useful thing for a relationship: listen, help, keep a plan, attempt a call, or make an appropriate apology or invitation.
If no safe relationship is available, take a step towards a group or service.
The activity review is recorded or kept for later, and you’ve taken one relationship or support step.

Lesson 64
Choose support without revisiting painful events
The child is father of the man.
William Wordsworth
Part 1
The present-day reaction
Past experiences may affect how you respond now, but this course can’t tell you what caused a current reaction. You don’t need to describe painful events to work on a present-day need.
If a connection to the past seems relevant, choose a reaction you can name today: becoming tense in an argument, withdrawing, or wanting to escape a difficult feeling.
Then choose a safe response for the present. You might orient yourself to the room, step away from an unsafe interaction, or contact someone appropriate.
Keep the reflection optional. You can skip it without a reason. If it becomes upsetting, stop and choose ordinary care or support.
There is no requirement to write a detailed account, revisit a memory, or prove you have found the root of porn use.
Part 2
What a course can’t provide
Structured trauma treatments have trained clinicians, defined procedures, and support.
For example, written exposure therapy described by the US Department of Veterans Affairs is a therapist-led treatment. A daily journaling exercise shouldn’t pretend to provide the same thing.
Suppose conflict makes you want to disappear into browsing. Today you could close the content, notice where you are, and decide when or with whom to discuss the conflict safely.
You can address that reaction without tracing it back through your entire history.
If no connection fits, say the topic doesn’t apply and continue the day. Not every habit needs a childhood explanation. The practical steps you’ve already prepared remain available.
Part 3
Care now

Today’s task is to prepare one present-day support option, or choose to skip. Use a gentle grounding action only if it’s comfortable. If the problem feels too distressing to manage alone, seek qualified help.
You don’t need to finish understanding the past before taking care of yourself now. Food, rest, safety, and appropriate support are available reasons for the next action.
It is never too late to be what you might have been.
George Eliot, often attributed
Today’s task
Choose support without revisiting painful events
This exercise is optional. You can name one present-day reaction and prepare a safe response, such as noticing the room, leaving an unsafe setting, or saving a qualified support contact.
Try gentle grounding only if comfortable.
You can also mark the topic as not relevant or skip without giving a reason. If reflection becomes upsetting, stop and choose care or support. No account of a past event is required.
A present-day response is prepared, or you’ve chosen to skip, stop, or mark the topic not relevant.

Lesson 65
Change one difficult setting
You are the average of the five people you spend the most time with.
Jim Rohn
Part 1
What keeps happening
Change one part of the setting that keeps making your difficult evenings harder. Start with something you control safely.

It may be a browsing routine, the place you work, a late-night conversation, or an account that keeps sending material you don’t want. Describe what happens repeatedly, then choose a proportionate change.
For example, working in bed might leave the laptop open when you’re tired. You could finish the specified work at a table and put the device away afterwards.
If the table isn’t available, close the work and change how the device is stored. Fit the action to the space you have.
Part 2
Proportionate changes
A contact may need a limit rather than a dramatic break. You might mute a channel or decline one kind of invitation.
If the situation is unsafe or complicated, get support before making a change. This lesson doesn’t require leaving a relationship, home, or job.
Avoid making a broad life decision from one difficult night. Look at the repeated facts and what you’ve already tried.
Sometimes the missing change is small; sometimes the problem needs advice, care, or more resources than a course can provide.
Part 3
Start today
Choose the first action and do it today if possible. If support must come first, make the enquiry.
If the setting can’t be changed immediately, prepare a response you can use within it, without blaming yourself for the constraint.
There may be no relevant setting to change. Keep what’s helping and record that no adjustment is needed. The calendar reaching a new lesson isn’t evidence that another rule is necessary.
After a chance to use the change, check whether it addressed the specific problem. Don’t ask whether your whole life is fixed.
Knowing that work now ends before browsing begins, or that a harmful channel is muted, gives you a clearer result to build on.
The first step toward getting somewhere is to decide that you are not going to stay where you are.
J. P. Morgan, attributed
Today’s task
Change one difficult setting
Choose one setting that repeatedly makes difficult evenings harder, if any. Change a feature you safely control: timing, device use, work location, or contact with a harmful channel.
If changing it is unsafe or complicated, request support first. If nothing fits, keep what’s helping and record that no change is needed.
You’ve made a safe adjustment or support step, or confirmed no change is needed. Leaving a home, job, or relationship isn’t required.

Lesson 66
Describe a mistake without an insult
No one can make you feel inferior without your consent.
Eleanor Roosevelt

items.t: “I missed the deadline.”
“I’m useless.”

atoms.t: Part 1
Criticism or insult
Separate useful criticism from an insult. “I missed the deadline” names an event. “I’m useless” makes a claim about the whole person.
Write the event, its consequence, and what needs attention. Keep responsibility in the sentence. If work was delayed, say so and choose the next step.
If an agreement was broken, consider the appropriate repair. Removing the insult doesn’t erase either.
Part 2
Speaking to yourself
Research by Ethan Kross and colleagues tested ways of speaking to oneself under stress.
In several experiments, using one’s name or non-first-person language affected responses to stressful tasks. This isn’t a treatment test for porn use.
You can try the idea if it makes a factual response easier: “Alex missed the task. What’s the next step?” Use your own name, or ordinary first-person wording if that feels more natural.

The sentence shouldn’t become a performance. “I watched longer than planned. I’ll close it now and prepare for bed” is enough. You don’t need to convince yourself you’re wonderful before taking the action.
Part 3
Keep the fact
Choose a recent judgement if one is available. What part is a fact, and what part is a sweeping conclusion? Keep the fact and remove the unsupported claim. Save the short response for Day 68.
If there is no harsh judgement today, describe an everyday difficulty plainly or mark the exercise as unnecessary. Don’t invent a mistake to practise being kinder.
Part 4
Then act
Then return to something useful. Take the repair step, meet a basic need, or ask for support. Rewriting the sentence repeatedly can become another way to postpone the action.

If self-criticism is severe, persistent, or linked to serious distress, seek qualified help. A factual sentence can help with a moment; it isn’t expected to carry every problem behind how you speak to yourself.
The greatest discovery of my generation is that a human being can alter his life by altering his attitudes.
William James, commonly attributed
Today’s task
Describe a mistake without an insult
Choose a recent harsh judgement if available. Write the event, actual consequence, and next action without the insult or unsupported claim about yourself.
Save the brief response for Day 68. Include a repair or support step if needed. If no harsh judgement fits, describe an everyday difficulty factually or mark the task unnecessary.
You’ve written the factual response or recorded that the pattern doesn’t apply. No new mistake is needed.

Lesson 67
When you feel bad about yourself
Hatred is blind.
Oscar Wilde
Part 1
When it feels pointless
Self-loathing can make an action feel pointless before you begin it. You may avoid a meal, a conversation, or work because the judgement says you don’t deserve another attempt.
Bring the judgement back to what you know. “I did something I regret” leaves room for a repair. “Everything about me is bad” goes beyond the event and gives you no instructions for what to do next.
Use yesterday’s factual response if it fits. Then choose one action the judgement has been preventing: eat, wash, keep a commitment, make appropriate contact, or ask for professional support.
The action can begin while the feeling remains.
Part 2
Ordinary contact
Suppose you watched longer than planned and now don’t want to answer a friend. You can reply about the plan you made without disclosing the entire episode.
The friend isn’t owed a confession, and you aren’t required to feel good about yourself before keeping ordinary contact.

If a real repair is needed, make it proportionate. An apology should address the person affected. It shouldn’t become a request that they reassure you repeatedly or take responsibility for the next attempt.
There may be no self-loathing problem today. Continue one normal act of care and leave the analysis aside. A course about this topic doesn’t need to make the topic part of every reader’s identity.
Part 3
Take the action once
Take the chosen action once. Afterwards, notice whether it helped you resume something important.
Don’t demand that it remove the judgement immediately. The meal or appointment can matter even while your thoughts remain harsh.
When self-hatred is persistent or overwhelming, get qualified support. If you’re in immediate danger, use urgent local help.
You can work on the behaviour you want to change while also receiving care for distress that deserves attention in its own right.
Nothing is more deceitful than the appearance of humility. It is often only carelessness of opinion, and sometimes an indirect boast.
Jane Austen
Today’s task
When you feel bad about yourself
Use the Day 66 example if it fits. Bring a broad judgement back to the facts and take one action it has been preventing: food, washing, a commitment, appropriate contact, or professional support.
If no such judgement fits, keep normal care and leave the analysis aside. Disclosure is optional and should be appropriate to the person and situation.
You’ve taken the fitting action or requested support.

Lesson 68
Check your response to self-criticism
Be kind, for everyone you meet is fighting a hard battle.
Often attributed to Plato
Part 1
A practical response
Self-compassion can be a practical response after a difficult moment. Describe what happened accurately, take care of what is needed, and choose a next step.
The experiments on Day 44 found that brief self-compassion exercises sometimes increased motivation to improve or make amends.
The lesson doesn’t require a warm feeling towards yourself. It asks whether the response helps you act without adding unnecessary punishment.
Part 2
Review your sentence
Review the sentence you wrote on Day 66. Did you use it? What happened next? Perhaps you ate, stopped browsing, or made a repair.
Perhaps you kept repeating the insult. Keep the result honest and adjust one detail if needed.
If you haven’t needed the response yet, read it once and name when you’d use it. That checks whether the wording is easy to remember.
It doesn’t show how it will help in a real difficult moment. Don’t create a mistake to get that information.

If self-criticism isn’t relevant, review the ordinary steps after a slip instead. The factual beginning might be enough: close the content, put the device away, and return to the next thing the hour needs.
Part 3
Make it easy to use
Keep the practice brief. If reflection makes you more distressed or turns into repeated checking, stop and choose an action or support. You don’t need a long account of why you feel the way you do.
Imagine saying the sentence after a tiring evening. Does it tell you what to do first?
If it’s full of reassuring claims you don’t believe, make it simpler. “That happened. I can put the phone away now” may be easier to use.
Today, finish with the next action rather than another paragraph about kindness.
Food, rest, repair, and appropriate help can be taken seriously without requiring you to settle every judgement about yourself first.

Keep what helped or change one awkward detail.
If you haven’t needed it, practise the short response once. If the topic doesn’t fit, keep the after-slip steps instead.
Add a note (optional)
If you want others to be happy, practice compassion. If you want to be happy, practice compassion.
Dalai Lama
Today’s task
Check your response to self-criticism
Review a real use of the Day 66 response if there has been one. Record what happened next and change one detail if needed.
If you haven’t needed it, read it once and name when you’d use it. If self-criticism doesn’t fit, check the after-slip steps instead. Keep this brief and stop if reflection becomes upsetting.
You’ve reviewed actual use or practised a suitable response without creating a mistake.

Lesson 69
Keep one manageable commitment
Trust thyself: every heart vibrates to that iron string.
Ralph Waldo Emerson
Part 1
Small enough to attempt
Choose a commitment small enough to attempt today. Give it a time or cue, prepare what it needs, and see what happens.
Use something useful: a short hobby session, an easy meal, a first piece of work, or a device rule that’s helping. You can keep an existing commitment rather than add another task.
Suppose you want to read after dinner. Put the book beside the chair and decide to read a few pages before the feed.
The promise is specific enough to follow and modest enough to fit a normal evening. If you’re unwell, rest may be the better commitment.
Part 2
Completed, changed, or missed
Afterwards, record completed, changed, or missed. If you changed it, say why.
If you missed it, ask what got in the way: forgetting, time, unavailable materials, or an activity that didn’t fit. Then choose the next reasonable chance.

A missed attempt doesn’t need extra punishment. Adding an hour of work to tomorrow may make the commitment even harder. A visible reminder or a smaller beginning may address the problem more directly.
Nor does one completed task establish that you’ll keep every future promise. Let the evidence stay the size it is.
You attempted this action and saw this result. Repeating useful commitments can give you more to rely on over time.
Part 3
Keep it simple
Keep the notes short. If recording becomes more demanding than the activity, simplify the record. The point is to understand whether the plan fits, then spend time doing it.
Today, make the attempt and decide what follows. You don’t have to announce a new identity or wait to feel fully trustworthy.
A clear action, an honest result, and another reasonable opportunity are enough to work with.
If the plan repeatedly fails because a larger difficulty is unresolved, ask for help with that difficulty rather than keep lowering your opinion of yourself.
Well done is better than well said.
Benjamin Franklin
Today’s task
Keep one manageable commitment
Choose one useful, modest action and give it a time or cue. Prepare the materials and attempt it. An existing commitment is fine.
Record completed, changed, or missed, with a practical reason if needed. If missed, choose the next realistic chance without adding punishment or restarting the course.
You’ve made the attempt and recorded the result, including an appropriate adjustment.

Lesson 70
Simplify the plan
Waste no more time arguing what a good man should be. Be one.
Marcus Aurelius
Part 1
What the course has added
Review what the course has added to your day. Keep the parts you can explain and use. Simplify the ones that have become more demanding than helpful.

You may have a phone rule, a response to urges, an activity, a few notes, and review reminders. Each should serve a purpose. You don’t need a large collection of techniques to prove you’re making an effort.
Ask which change has actually helped. Keep it. Ask which one has an awkward beginning. Make that beginning easier. If an optional task gives you no useful information or action, consider stopping it.
Part 2
Cut what isn’t helping
Suppose nightly tracking now takes half an hour and leads to repeated checking. A brief note about whether the phone stayed out of bed may be enough.
The record should help you make decisions without taking the evening it’s meant to protect.
Or perhaps the activity schedule contains more sessions than you can attend. Keep the one you value and can realistically repeat. Missing the other sessions isn’t a reason to abandon the useful one.
If everything has a clear purpose and fits, leave it alone. The exercise doesn’t require deleting a task just to produce an answer. You can confirm the plan is manageable.
Part 3
A plan for a busy evening
Keep professional care separate from optional course demands. Discuss treatment changes with the relevant clinician. A lesson about simplifying isn’t advice to stop prescribed care or medication.
Today, leave a plan you could use on a normal, busy evening. Put the first actions where you’ll find them. Retain review dates that will help with an actual decision.
Then use some of the time for the rest of life. You don’t need to make self-improvement the new activity that fills every gap.
The course should support sleep, work, pleasure, relationships, and care, rather than become another thing that repeatedly crowds them out.
Become who you are.
Friedrich Nietzsche
Today’s task
Simplify the plan
Review your plan. Keep something that helps, simplify something awkward if needed, and stop an optional demand only if it has no useful purpose.
If every part fits, retain it. Discuss changes to professional treatment with the clinician; don’t treat it as an optional course demand. Leave a plan you can explain and use on a busy evening.
The plan is reviewed and manageable. Another improvement project isn’t required.

Lesson 71
Use what your notes show
Know thyself.
Inscription at the Temple of Apollo at Delphi
Part 1
Read a few entries
Read two or three entries from your plan. Choose ones that contain something you can use: what happened before browsing, a response you tried, or an activity you attended.
Look for a repeated difficulty and a response that helped. If the record doesn’t support either, say so.
A few entries aren’t enough to explain your whole personality, and you don’t need a tidy pattern to continue.
Perhaps the same problem appears after late shifts. Food and an earlier stopping time may be worth preparing.
Perhaps you keep the phone rule easily but avoid the work waiting afterwards. That points towards the task itself, not another charger location.
Part 2
Adjust the week
Use the information to adjust the coming week. Keep the change that’s helping and work on the detail that keeps getting in the way. One adjustment is easier to assess than a complete redesign.
If the notes are thin, choose one observation to collect next week. You could record when searching begins, whether the phone stays out of bed, or what happens after an urge.
Pick the information you’ll need for a decision. Unknown is a valid answer until you have it.
Keep the device placement and rules that help. You don’t need to keep changing them because a lesson asks you to review. Confirming that they still fit can be the result.
Part 3
When you need more help

If the record shows worsening control or serious effects on daily life, use that information to seek qualified help. Understanding yourself includes recognising when the current level of support isn’t enough.
Today, make the week’s plan reflect what you actually know. Then begin one useful action from it.
Save only the notes that will help you remember or review. A plan that you can read and follow is more useful than a lengthy explanation you rarely open.
To know oneself is the beginning of wisdom.
Aristotle, traditionally attributed

Use what your notes show
Read two or three useful entries. Identify one repeated difficulty and one response that helped if the record supports them. Use that information for the coming week.
If the record is thin, choose one brief observation to collect instead. Keep the existing setup when it fits, and take a support step if the record shows the current help isn’t enough.

Lesson 72
Choose what you can do now
My formula for greatness in a human being is amor fati: that one wants nothing to be different.
Friedrich Nietzsche
Part 1
Accepting what happened
You can’t undo a past decision. You may still be able to repair a consequence or decide what happens next.
The Stoic idea often called amor fati can be read as accepting that the event has happened. Epictetus discusses responding to events we can’t fully control.
You don’t have to welcome harm, excuse another person’s behaviour, or feel grateful for a painful experience to take a present action.

head: Already settled
Still within reach
rows: An apology and a new booking

atoms.t: Choose an everyday event if this reflection is useful. What is already settled? What remains within reach? A missed appointment might allow an apology and a new booking.
A lost evening might allow food and sleep now. Some things have no direct repair, and continuing a valued activity may be the next step.
Part 2
Gratitude is optional
Gratitude is a separate option, not an obligation. Emmons and McCullough tested gratitude-focused diary exercises and found benefits for some measures, but not every outcome improved in every study.
Those findings don’t require thanking someone who harmed you or making every setback into a lesson.
If you’d like, notice something you appreciate in the present. Keep it specific: a person who helped, a meal, or a place you can rest. If gratitude feels forced, leave it aside.
The reflection is also optional. You can skip it if it becomes upsetting or unhelpful. Choose ordinary care or appropriate support instead. There’s no reason to retell a painful event for the course.
Part 3
One proportionate action
Today, take one proportionate action. Make the repair, begin an activity, or ask for help. Let that action end the reflection for now.

Acceptance doesn’t need to settle how you feel about the past. It can simply mean working from what has happened, without repeatedly waiting for a different past before using the choices available today.

The willing are led by fate, the reluctant dragged.
Cleanthes, preserved by Seneca
Today’s task
Choose what you can do now
If helpful, choose an everyday past event and distinguish what has happened from what you can do now. Take a proportionate repair or present-day action.
If no repair fits, choose a valued activity. If reflection is upsetting or unhelpful, skip and choose care or support. Gratitude, forgiveness, and retelling a painful event aren’t required.

Lesson 73
Reserve time for what matters
You could leave life right now. Let that determine what you do and say and think.
Marcus Aurelius
Part 1
Make room this week
What have you been meaning to give more time to? A person, a skill, an enjoyable activity, or a responsibility may come to mind.
The question “What if I had five years left?” can help some people choose.
For others, thinking about mortality is upsetting or unnecessary. You can use a simpler question: what do I want to make room for this week?
Part 2
Reserve a block
Choose one answer and reserve a realistic block in the next seven days. An hour may fit; fifteen minutes may be more honest.
If another person is involved, make an invitation and allow them to choose. If a booking is needed, check the details.
Suppose you keep saying you’d like to see an old friend. Suggest a day and an activity rather than write “relationships” as a goal.
If the person isn’t available, choose another date or a different valued activity. Their reply isn’t something the course can require.

Begin a small part today: prepare materials, send the invitation, or make the booking. The future block should have a practical beginning rather than depend on becoming a different kind of person first.
Part 3
Check afterwards

Set a check for after the block. Did it happen? Did it fit? Would you give it time again? We’ll revisit it on Day 84 if it’s occurred by then. Otherwise, leave the reminder for after the actual session.
You can reuse something already in the week. The task doesn’t require a dramatic new priority. Keeping a commitment to someone you value may be enough.
When the block arrives, give it your attention as far as circumstances allow. If something interrupts it, record that and choose another chance.
The purpose is to make time for what matters, without turning a missed appointment into another reason to abandon the plan.
It is not death that a man should fear, but he should fear never beginning to live.
Marcus Aurelius
Today’s task
Reserve time for what matters
Choose a person, activity, or responsibility you want to give more time to. Reserve a realistic block in the next seven days and begin a small part today, or make the needed invitation or booking.
Set a review after the block: did it happen, did it fit, and will you repeat it? Save it for Day 84 if due then, or for after the actual session.
The time and review are scheduled and a first step is taken. Mortality reflection is optional.

Lesson 74
Begin an activity you postponed
Carpe diem, quam minimum credula postero.
Horace
Part 1
Ten to twenty minutes
Begin a part of the activity you’ve been postponing. Use yesterday’s choice if it fits.
Choose ten to twenty minutes of something available today. Read, practise, walk, prepare a meal, or make a necessary enquiry.
If the activity depends on another person or booking, make that arrangement and prepare what you can.
Part 2
Enough to begin

Lesson 82

Part 1
Lessons from other addictions
Other addictions can offer useful parallels about access, support, and returning after setbacks. They also have differences in risk and treatment that shouldn’t be borrowed casually.
In a GamCare account, David describes returning to gambling after three years away from it. His later help included therapy, debt advice, family support, and self-exclusion.
It’s one person’s story. It shows several kinds of help addressing several kinds of difficulty, rather than one technique carrying everything.
NIDA’s guidance on substance use also describes renewed use as a possible reason to resume or modify treatment.
This isn’t proof that porn use and substance dependence are the same. Medication, withdrawal care, and other treatment decisions belong with appropriate professionals.
Part 2

If help is needed now, send the request or make the call. Don’t leave a prepared message unsent because the course hasn’t ended.
